speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of pressing and urgent necessity pursuant to Standing Order 43. It concerns the plight of Danylo Shumuk, a Soviet citizen who has been imprisoned in the U.S.S.R. for over 27 years for activities that would constitute no crime in a free society. Given that Mr. Shumuk is living in great physical and mental deprivation, and that he is nearly 64 years of age, and that he has many relatives in Canada who are willing to sponsor his entry to Canada, and given that he has been adopted as a prisoner of conscience by Amnesty International since 1972, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the minister instruct the Canadian delegation to this fall's Belgrade Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe to publicly raise the plight of Danylo Shumuk, and take all steps to secure his release from the Soviet Union.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we can get a better legal opinion than that offered by the Prime Minister, and we have it. That legal opinion is that this order in council, passed by the government to protect itself from scrutiny, bars this party, any Canadian citizen or any member of parliament from proceeding in the courts or having an inquiry started under the Combines Investigation Act. I asked the Prime Minister to have that stopped. I have asked him three times to give us a simple, clear, unequivocal commitment that he will remove this obstacle directly.
I ask, why did the Prime Minister, as head of the government, choose not to follow the example set by the government of Australia which, when faced with a problem similar to that cited by the Prime Minister, simply passed legislation to prevent extra-territorial demands for information? This order in council, in contrast to what is happening in Australia where they respect the rights of their legislators and of the citizens, stops domestic inquiry into domestic matters. If the Prime Minister of Canada wanted to prevent extraterritorial demands for information, he could have done as Australia did and passed legislation. Why did he not do that? Why did he, instead, bring in this odious order in council which seriously restricts the rights and capacities to inquire of this parliament and of the people of Canada?

speechtext:
Order, please. Before allowing the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) to state his question of privilege, I should like to deal with the question of privilege raised yesterday by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin). The hon. member interpreted correctly the preliminary opinion I gave yesterday, which I now confirm.
I should like to make reference to a ruling I made on March 17 of this year which was with reference to a very similar question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Peace River. I think it is important to understand that the Chair should not attempt to decipher legal opinions and decide between one and another legal opinion. Furthermore, the Chair should not attempt to decide whether or not government action is technically or legally justified.
The Chair has to decide on questions of procedure and whether they extend into the area of privilege. Privilege, while it goes beyond procedure into substance, does in fact, for obvious reasons, have a strict definition. That strict definition has been repeated many times in the past, and it relates to actual interference with a member of parliament in the discharge of his or her duties. In fact, the hon. member for Peace River referred to this order in council as being a potential interference in that regard. Were it an actual interference, it would be a different situation so far as the argument is concerned. At the moment, I think all hon. members will agree that if there is the interference described in the terms put forward yesterday by the hon. member for Peace River, it is potential in nature and not actual. Therefore, I reiterate the ruling I gave on March 17 in respect of some regulations that were passed at that time which had a similar potential effect.
While members are expressing fear that the effect of this order in council might be to restrict them in the transportation, use or release of documents in their possession, unless the restriction has taken place I believe it would be an unwarranted extension of the definition of privilege for the Chair to indicate that the danger of that taking place, rather than the actuality of it, constituted a question of privilege. Therefore, 1 set aside the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Peace River yesterday.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. It pertains to a very serious

accusation made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald). He has totally mismanaged the Canadian economy, and rather than acknowledging that, he makes accusations about hon. members when they try to put the record straight. The minister said earlier in the question period that what 1 said was false and that I knew it was false. That is a serious accusation for one member to make about another member of the House, and 1 do not take it lightly.
I want to document for the minister what other ministers have said on the subject of the failure of the budget, including the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and then I will let the Minister of Finance repeat his accusation, if he wants to. The point I made during the question period is that a variety of ministers of the Crown have acknowledged the failure of the budget to create jobs by stimulating the private sector. It was that which the Minister of Finance said was a false description of what had been said. I see he is nodding his head.
I have reference here to three ministers who support the question I put to the Minister of Finance. The judgment of these three ministers is that the budget has failed. The first judgment was made by the President of Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) in a speech, appropriately enough, to the Canadian Manufacturers Association in Toronto on July 12. He was talking about the failure of the Canadian economy to create jobs and, related to that and entirely appropriately, to growing feelings of disunity in the country. At that time the President of Treasury Board said, and I quote from his text:
-pressure is building to substitute public spending on direct public sector job creation . . . and there will be very heavy pressure indeed if significant private sector employment increase, through expanded or new activity, is not forthcoming soon.
The whole thrust of that part of the speech of the President of Treasury Board was that the private sector was not producing the jobs that the government expected it would in its earlier budget. In addition to the President of the Treasury Board, 1 would like to quote the Minister of Finance himself. In a newspaper article which appeared in the Toronto Star on July 22 we find the following:
The federal government may be forced to spend more on emergency job creation if business investment doesn't pick up soon, says finance minister Donald Macdonald.
"We will have to make a decision by the end of this month," he told the Star yesterday. If government projections indicate investment is not going to improve in the next few months, "perhaps we'll have to step in."
Later in the same article it says:
In his March budget, Macdonald provided $1.2 billion in tax cuts for companies in the hope they would expand and create more jobs.
Yesterday, he admitted the strategy wasn't working.
The story continues in the same vein. Finally, I would like to refer to the Prime Minister. In the same article pertaining to the failure of the budget to create jobs, in the judgment of the Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister is quoted as having said earlier in the week-

In addition, the quotations read by the hon. gentleman do not support that whatsoever. The quotations he read are, "We may be forced to spend more if business does not pick up soon," and, "Perhaps we will have to step in". Both quotations refer to possible future measures. In other words, that is what I said to the hon. gentlemen-indeed, also in response to the hon. gentleman's colleague in this House-and I think it is significant that the Leader of the NDP chose to refer to press reports rather than statements actually made by me in response to his colleague right here in the House.

However, at the end of this month I will be having an analysis of the first quarter returns, and as much as is available on the second quarter returns, made to determine whether in the absence of private expenditure some additional public expenditure-additional to that announced by my colleague the other day-will be desirable for this coming winter.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which arises from the ruling Your Honour made on the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin). As I understood the thrust of your ruling, you came down against the motion my colleague proposed to move, on the basis that there was no infringement, other than an apprehended infringement, of the rights of members of parliament with respect to the regulation concerning the security of information regulation with respect to the uranium question.
My question of privilege is this. In my case there has already been an infringement, in my view, of my right to perform as a member of parliament in this House. I requested a large Toronto law firm to review the documentation I had at my disposal, to determine to what extent they felt an offence had been committed and, second, to what extent they felt that offence had been committed not only by officials of companies in the private sector but by certain members of the government as well. They considered the question. Upon my drawing their attention to the regulation to which 1 have referred, they said they felt they could no longer continue to even review the documentation, or to advise me on the subject, as they themselves might be charged under the provisions of the Atomic Energy Control Act.
The chap with whom 1 was dealing said he would discuss it with two of his partners. He telephoned me again in two hours and said they both felt unanimously that there was no way they could participate in the formation of an opinion with respect to this matter. Within one hour, the documents in their entirety were returned to my Toronto office.

subtopic: MR. STEVENS-RULING BY MR. SPEAKER ON QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE OF MR. BALDWIN
speechtext: Obviously, you did not have a case.

subtopic: MR. STEVENS-RULING BY MR. SPEAKER ON QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE OF MR. BALDWIN

Mr. Speaker, the second infringement occurred in this manner. I planned to go to the United States in order to review certain documents which had been made available to us in the United States. Members of a Toronto law firm agreed to go down to attend and review the documents with me. Subsequently, within 12 hours of our leaving for the United States, they told me they could not go on the trip. They felt they could not review the documents because of the impact of the regulations to which we have been referring.
In short, in two instances legal counsel of two large law firms in Toronto said that they felt the regulation was so all-embracing and so wide that they would risk being charged even if they simply reviewed the documentation with a view to giving me an opinion as to what the legal consequences might be of actions taken by certain individuals as revealed in those documents. That, in essence, is my question of privilege. If you
[Mr. Speaker.)
find a prima facie case, I propose to move the following motion:
That the question of my inability as a member of this House to consult with counsel on the question of a uranium cartel and seek legal opinion as to action being taken with reference thereto be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

Similarly, the point arises in connection with the hon. member's going out of the country to have access-

No person who has in his possession or under his control any note, document, or other written or printed material in any way related to conversations, discussions or meetings that took place between January 1, 1972, and December 31, 1975, involving that person or any other person or any government, Crown corporation, agency or other organization in respect of the production, import, export, transportation, refining, possession, ownership, use or sale of uranium or its derivatives or compounds, shall
(a) release any such note, document or material, or disclose or communicate
the contents thereof to any person, government, Crown corporation, agency or
other organization unless
(1) he is required to do so by or under a law of Canada, or (ii) he does so with the consent-
It is not just a mere question of procedure. This is not a mere tabling of documents. What has happened to the public of Canada and to this House over which Your Honour presides is that by your ruling, a member of parliament, before he would have a question of privilege, would have to commit an offence and be in jail-that is, before he would have a question of privilege with respect to this matter.

Order, please. Before the hon. member interprets my language for me-and 1 want to give him full amplitude to develop his argument-I want to make it clear that he must establish something that comes within the four corners of privilege as we have known them within the classic definition of privilege, the interference with a member in the performance of his duties.
The hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) indicated that he had documentation, sent it to his lawyers and his lawyers said they could not give him an opinion on it. That is their opinion. Surely the Chair is not called upon to say whether that is right or wrong. The member was not in a position to say he attempted to get documentation which was refused to him on the basis of this order in council, or that it was documentation that had been refused on grounds of confidentiality or relationship with other government, or one of several other standards. Bear in mind that in applications for documents by members of the House of Commons there are several grounds upon which the government has, and does, regularly refuse production of documents to members of this House.
If an application is made for documentation with respect to a certain negotiation, the application is made in this House

August 5, 1977
Privilege-Mr. W. Baker
and the minister rises in his place and says they will not produce that document because it relates to confidential negotiations, does the member rise in his place and say that he is asking for a document, he cannot get it and that is a question of privilege? Surely not. There must be something more than the inability of members to be able to get the tabling of that document.
The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) stood in his place today-by way of a point of order, by the way- and said to the minister the honourable thing to do would be to stand up and agree to table all of these documents. The minister said, "Of course I cannot agree to table all documents until I know what documents they are and what restrictions they might be under." Does that constitute a question of privilege? How can I bring that within the definition of privilege? I am not in any way saying that the member has to go and steal the documents from the minister. Surely that is not an accurate interpretation of the language I have used. Surely there must be more than some sort of refusal to produce documents on the classic grounds that have been known in the past.

That is not Your Honour's function; I admit that. The point is the lawyer, the solicitor or counsel who made the statement that the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) has indicated made the statement regardless of where he stands on the question of right or wrong.
The facts are now that the hon. member for York-Simcoe, by Your Honour's ruling and, indeed, any other member of this House of Commons, even when faced with a legal opinion that is wrong, that that particular lawyer could not give an opinion, is now in the position where his privileges as a member of parliament to investigate, as a member of parliament, as a citizen to involve himself in the court process, however you want to cut it, is denied access to documents and to opinion on those documents by this order in council which the Leader of the Opposition has rightfully described as an odious order in council. That is the situation in which we find ourselves.
This is not an ordinary production of documents. I asked this question specifically, admittedly not in the question period but as a point of order. It would have been grand if it had been in the question period, but it was not. It was outside the question period. The question was answered. The question was

not answered on the grounds Your Honour suggests. It was answered on the basis that the question was frivolous and I knew it. There was an absolute refusal to produce those documents.

It is on the record that it was frivolous. The disparaging remarks followed. On the basis of this order in council, we are now being denied the documents. That is out of the mouth of the minister. In these unusual circumstances, I do not know how anyone including, with respect, Your Honour, could call this an ordinary matter of production of documents, in view of what has happened. What has clearly happened is that I, as a member of parliament, in the circumstances of the last few days in the face of order in council by the government, have been denied access here in the House of Commons to documents, according to one legal opinion, right or wrong, upon which you do not have to decide. The solicitor could not give an opinion to a member of parliament to permit him to carry out his duties.
I want those documents as a matter of my right as a member of parliament. It is not an ordinary production. In view of what has happened, I do not think it can be handled in any other way. Therefore, in view of the refusal and in view of what I have said, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin):
That this House declare that the order in council No. SOR 76-644 is not binding on members of the House with regard to proceedings in the House or any committee thereof or their counsel and that for the purpose of such proceedings, despite the provisions of such order in council, all documents or copies may be obtained, produced and used in connection with any inquiry into questions of privilege or into the legality and propriety of the actions of the government and minister and others in the establishment of a uranium cartel.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I make one very brief comment before a final ruling is made or is reserved, though there is little time left for reservation today. Your Honour will take note, as a member of the profession to which 1 have the honour to belong as well, of the punitive nature of this order in council. It is not just a civil matter; this is an order in council passed under the Atomic Energy Control Act. Any offence against that act or any of the regulations under the act carries with it a very heavy penalty. I do not have the act here, but I examined it the other day. There are very heavy penalties attached to any infraction or breach of that act or regulation.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the minute that I-or, indeed, my friend for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker), the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) or the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens)-go to anyone to secure possession of these documents and I have them in my possession, I commit an offence against this order in council. This goes back to the case that Your Honour will remember we discussed in committee, of Strauss, the father of the House in the United Kingdom. I remember that in that case the original decision was against Strauss; but ten years later, in a report of the committee proceedings in 1966 and 1967, my recollection is that the procedure committee in the House in England at that time made it quite plain that any attempt which was made in that case, by threats against a member of the House, to inhibit him in the carrying out of his functions and duties constituted, in their opinion, a breach of privilege.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what could be a greater threat to us than the contents of this order in council? It constitutes a threat to every member of this House that if they dare to secure, without the permission-the very selective permission, probably-of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie), possession of a document for the purpose of proceeding in the House or out of the House, it would immediately render them liable to a criminal proceeding and to the imposition of a very heavy penalty.
I suggest to Your Honour that there could be nothing more conducive to inhibiting members of this House in the discharge of their duty than the fact that they know-and 1 intend to pursue this matter when I leave the House today-that if I come into possession of some of these documents, not second or third rate copies out of the proceedings in Washington, but the original documents themselves, that if I go to a member of this cartel, ask for a document and they show it to me and for some reason are prepared to give it to me, then I have committed an offence. How can I prepare a case for proceeding in this House?

The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) has very accurately and coolly described the circumstances under which this order in council, in his view, constitutes a threat to his ability to function as a member of the House of Commons. I can understand that interpretation.
Again I say that if the hon. member was standing in his place and saying to me that he has done what he says he might do, and that he had met with that kind of response, I would be dealing with a much different question from the one I am dealing with at the present time. I maintain that so long as the matter remains in the potential, as opposed to being in the actual, the Chair would be making an unwarranted extension of privilege to accept the matter as a question of privilege.
With respect to the application by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) which we are specifically dealing with here, the basis of his question of privilege is the statement made by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) today that he could not give the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton a blanket assurance that he would table all of the documents which relate to these transactions. speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-ANSWER OF MINISTER OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on the same question. Let me preface my remarks by saying that since the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) has now amended his original position and has at least asked to consider requests for specific documents, we will take him up on that offer. 1 can advise the minister that it will be a very long list, and we would like to have a very expeditious reply.
We would also expect to have the kind of consent which would allow the parliament and people of Canada to get to the bottom of this question. I repeat what my colleague for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) has said, that access to information which will make a debate in this House useful and effective will, of course, be a condition precedent to our agreeing to a debate, because we do not intend to have a debate in which the information is hidden away in the back pocket of the minister.
If I might briefly repeat what others of my colleagues have said in argument on the question of privilege, we are not asking at all that Your Honour come to some decision on the competence of a legal opinion that two senior, respected firms in the city of Toronto felt constrained from participating in any way in any activity which had to do with these documents. Your Honour is not being asked to judge whether or not they were right. The point at issue here, with the greatest respect, is that the existence of this order in council prohibits, and has

August 5, 1977
Privilege-Mr. W. Baker
prohibited, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens)- it is not a theoretical matter; it is not potential or a threat; it is something that has happened-from seeking the kind of external advice regarding a complicated matter which he requires to have in order to carry out his responsibilities as an effective member of the House of Commons of Canada.
Again I emphasize that this is not a threat; it is not something which is potential. This is something which has happened to the hon. member for York-Simcoe on two occasions with respect to two separate, respected, substantial law firms in the city of Toronto. Their interpretation-which is an interpretation by very reputable counsel-of this order in council is such that it prevents them from giving a member the information that he requires to carry out his functions as effectively as he would want to in the House of Commons. As the hon. member for York-Simcoe has indicated, this is clearly one of those cases. This is even more the case in an atmosphere which has been developed deliberately by members of the government when in answer to any request for an inquiry into any kind of question they ask the members on this side to make a charge before they will divulge any information.
The hon. member for York-Simcoe, in anticipation that this latest attempt at a cover-up would bring forth the same response as earlier attempts at cover-up, went to legal counsel to seek advice in order to be in a position to function in the House of Commons within the ground rules the government is trying to impose upon this House. The fact that a member of parliament is precluded by this order in council from seeking the kind of expert advice he needs to carry out his duties is a clear interference with his rights. I should like to make two other brief points.

speechtext: I am informed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as follows: yes. (a) and (b). The quotations in question 70 are accurate but are out of context. Mr. Thogerson's letter is an internal memorandum that is part of a free and frank internal exchange on the contents of RCI broadcasts. The quotes from Mr. Thogerson's memo are part of Mr. Thogerson's critical response to the evaluation. This memo, in its proper context as an internal exchange of programming criticisms, is part of a normal interchange of views within the service.

subsubtopic: RADIO CANADA INTERNATIONAL
speechtext:
1.	Did Mr. Alan Brown, Director of Radio Canada International, circulate an internal memo dated May 12, 1976, under the heading: "Target Area Desks and Central Programming: Preliminary Steps"?
2.	Did this memo contain in part these words "no more so-called news backgrounders are to be written by Radio Canada International employees" and, if so, what are the reasons (a) CBC personnel were abruptly ordered not to do such a thing (b) background information to the news was considered suddenly undesirable?
3.	Did this memo also contain in part the words "Of course no commentaries will be written in-house on political or economic matters under whatever disguise" and, if so (a) what are the reasons justifying the forbidding of comments on political or economic matters on the CBC's international service (b) is it now CBC or government policy to censor from Canadian broadcasts to other countries items of a political or economic nature?
4.	Did the memo also state in part "a press review will then be written by Mr. Cote (I suggest at least three times a week) referring to both the French language and English language press-but the selection will be made by Mr. Cote" and, if so (a) what is the full name and job designation of Mr. Cote (b) for what reason, has this one individual been given exclusive judgement and right to decide what excerpts from the English and French language press will be broadcast to foreign listeners (c) what is Mr. Cote's employment history with the CBC and what are his qualifications for such exclusive power?

subsubtopic: RADIO CANADA INTERNATIONAL
speechtext:
I am informed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as follows: 1. Yes.
2.	Yes. (a) Radio Canada International seeks to reflect the spectrum of representative Canadian opinion on events, but should not, through its staff employees, have an editorial stance of its own. It was felt that a separate program element, referred to as a news backgrounder, had occasionally been susceptible to the inclusion of commentary by some staff employees and should, therefore, be replaced by a commentary
August 5, 1977

by freelancers. In addition, since CBC news policy precludes the inclusion of the staff news writer's own opinion in desk copy prepared for news bulletins proper, specific background facts only, (needed to explain a Canadian story to foreigners and to bring out its significance) would be incorporated by news-room staff as part of the news bulletin. News backgrounders, because of their length, are not a part of the news bulletin, but follow it in the slot where commentaries also normally appear. Where it would be difficult to deal with an event in the news without more extended explanation, either a backgrounder or commentary could continue, as had always been the case, to be dealt with in French or English by freelance commentators whose material would be available for translation by all foreign language sections, (b) Background information to the news is, of course, not considered undesirable. The policy is aimed at providing more background, using the most varied and knowledgeable sources.
3.	Yes. (a) The fact that commentaries were no longer to be written by the one or two staff members who occasionally did so does not mean that no commentaries, including those on political or economic matters, were to be broadcast by freelance commentators. The purpose of the memo was, on the contrary, to specify the duties of staff members and to widen the variety of commentary available through freelancers, thus ensuring the use of the best specialist expertise. Not only would the various language sections continue to have available commentaries written by freelance commentators in the official languages of Canada, English and French, for subsequent translation to the appropriate language, but the diversity of opinion available in Canada would be increasingly reflected by expanding the list of available authoritative freelance commentators. (b) No.
4.	Yes. Mr. Cote was given the editorial function of selection under the general direction of the assistant program director, (a) Lucien Cote, information resources officer, (b) It is normal for one person to compile a press review. Mr. Cote was given the responsibility because he is well informed on Canadian events and has a distinguished journalistic background. Since he is fluently bilingual, Mr. Cote has access to the contents of the English and French language press, (c) Mr. Cote is a highly experienced broadcaster and journalist. He has worked in the national service of the CBC, both in radio and in TV, and in the international service, or RCI.

speechtext:
I am informed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as follows: 1. A fairly elaborate program evaluation process was begun in September 1975 and between that time and February 1976 all language sections, including French and English sections, had undergone a preliminary evaluation. In the case of languages inaccessible to some members of the evaluating committees, an outside evaluation was commissioned to provide an additional element to the retranslations of program material available. The evaluations, internal and commissioned, are part of an ongoing process. As part of these evaluations, and on instructions from the director of Radio Canada International, Mr. England requested an evaluation of a number of Dr. Yaroshevsky's freelance contributions to the Russian section. Mr. Mogiljansky in his letter of May 25, 1976 quoted a memorandum from Mr. England as follows "The evaluation was undertaken by an outsider who is aware of our mandate", (a) The name and address of the evaluator cannot be revealed for obvious internal reasons, (b) The evaluator had experience in broadcasting, a distinguished academic career and knowledge of the Russian language, (c) The director of Radio Canada International in consultation with Mr. England and another member of his staff, (d) The phrase "is aware of our mandate"

August 5, 1977
Order Paper Questions
means that the evaluator understood Radio Canada International's strategic objective as approved by the board of directors of the CBC in 1973. It reads "Radio Canada International is directed by the CBC to provide a program service designed to attract an international awareness of Canada and the Canadian identity by distributing, through shortwave and other means, programs which reflect the realities and quality of Canadian life and culture, Canada's national interests and policies and the spectrum of Canadian viewpoints on national and international affairs."
2.	Yes. (a) to (j) Yes, it contained the remarks quoted. However, it must be understood that the evaluator's remarks, as quoted in part in 2(a) to (j), were one of several internal evaluations and had no status as CBC policy.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: CANADIAN FLAX STRAW
speechtext: Is the government aware of the reports that Canadian flax straw has been used to the limit of its availability for making fine paper products and, if so, is the government giving consideration to ensuring that more of this product is produced in the coming crop year?

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: CANADIAN FLAX STRAW
speechtext:
In so far as Agriculture Canada is concerned: Yes. Flax straw presently used for making fine paper products is a by-product of flax seed production and current prices for flax straw do not provide an incentive for producers to increase flax production. Increases in flax acreage cannot be encouraged solely to provide more straw. In addition to the research conducted and supported by Agriculture Canada, as outlined in the answer to Question 1,255, the government is working with producers to investigate possible production and market possibilities of special fibre flax varieties. Government officials have met with flax producers and some members of the Flaxseed Growers of Western Canada have been to a meeting held in Ottawa to discuss the topic. Also, a group of producers and researchers were sponsored on a mission to Europe to investigate European production and utilization of flax fibre.
In so far as the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce is concerned: Presently a limited amount of flaxseed straw is being collected and used for the production of fine paper products. The collection and further processing of flax straw is being examined as a complementary source of revenue for flax growers. To this end, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce has collaborated with the Flax Growers of Western Canada by funding a mission to western Europe to conduct trials on the production of flax fibre from Canadian flax straw, to evaluate processing technologies and processing equipment available and to evaluate market potential. It should also be noted that the department is assisting in a major way in the establishment of the "P.O.S." Pilot Plant Corporation in Saskatoon which has, as the prime objective, the value-added processing of grains and oilseeds including flax.

["An hon. member mentions rule by regulation. The government's actions in the area of energy are but another example of that rule. I do not think we have emphasized sufficiently in this debate the matter of Canada's security of future energy supplies. If we are to import about half our energy supplies, a substantial proportion will be shipped via the Indian Ocean and round South Africa. We shall be highly dependent on a number of foreign powers for our energy supplies. This, in addition to our economic difficulties, is a most serious problem to those of us who live in northern latitudes.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, it is very much in our interest to work together with the United States to make possible the construction of a northern pipeline. While we can be instrumental in making available to the United States sizable quantities of its own energy supplies, we can at the same time, probably by using the Dempster route, eventually bring into use our Mackenzie Delta and Beaufort Sea gas.
On reflecting on the events of the past months, after having visited recently the Mackenzie Delta, something I have done many times, I am impressed by a number of facts. For example, both natives and whites alike told me and my colleagues, when we visited the Delta, that Mr. Justice Berger's report does not properly represent the views of the northern people. The reason is, I think, that the views expressed to Mr. Justice Berger were largely those of a group of experts from Toronto, who arrived in the north on an aircraft ahead of Mr. Justice Berger and persuaded the natives as to what they should say. These same gentlemen probably wrote their reports right at the University of Toronto. We asked businessmen in the north why they did not put forward their views; or, why were we hearing from them views which had not been expressed to Mr. Justice Berger? The reason is this: the experts from Toronto were funded directly and indirectly by the government. They had funds which enabled them to sit at the hearings for days on end and to buy airline tickets which
Northern Gas Pipeline
are expensive items in northern communities. But the small businessmen, the young people who were enterprising and had staked their future in the north, had no chance to express their views, because they had neither the time nor the money to do it.
I can hardly fail to remind the House that Mr. Justice Berger himself at one time was an elected representative and formerly the leader of the New Democratic Party in British Columbia. As one northerner put it, asking Mr. Justice Berger to report on matters in the north is akin to appointing a cardinal to head a commission on abortion.
What are this country's energy reserves, and what are our potential sources of supply? We have a good deal of potential for supplies in Alberta. We have potential supplies off the east coast, but in deep water and probably cannot extract those supplies with presently known technology. I expect we shall need to learn new technologies. We have the Alberta oil sands and the heavy oils in Alberta. But the frontier area most likely to yield energy supplies immediately is the Mackenzie Delta.
We shall need all of this country's energy reserves. All will be required, each in their own time. The development of some can be hurried; the development of others cannot be. Huge sums of money will be required for exploration in our provinces and off the east coast. In view of the enormous costs of these developments, we shall need to time them carefully. Today we have known reserves in our western Arctic areas. The reports of the National Energy Board make clear that this area is the next and most important source which should be tapped for Canadian energy needs.
The projected production from the Mackenzie Delta would meet the growth in Canada's energy needs for less than two years. That should make it clear we shall need all our energy resources. We cannot stand aside at this time, awaiting the development of the oil sands, or the heavy oil reserves. We must make use of our present opportunity to bring on stream Mackenzie Delta gas.
It has been said in this debate that by agreeing to the pipeline we shall do the United States a favour. Before I deal with the point let me draw attention to the outstanding job done for many years by the Canadian Arctic gas group. This government told it to get to work and undertake studies in thousands of important areas. The group did its work well. It conducted undoubtedly one of the most thorough studies ever undertaken on northern ecological and transportation matters.
I ask again, who will be dealt a favour? I say that, yes, we can help the United States, and it is important for us to do so. But I also suggest this project is greatly to Canada's advantage. Today we desperately need the economic stimulus of this pipeline and its construction projects. This, of course, is largely due to the mess that our country is in as a result of the economic mismanagement of the government sitting opposite.
We cannot afford to build our own pipeline at the present time from our western Arctic reserves because they are not large enough. However, the Alaska-Yukon line which is pro-
80020-50 Vi", "August 5, 1977
Northern Gas Pipeline
posed by the Foothills group in Calgary to build their line within 480 miles of our reserves brings our reserves within reasonable distance of a major transportation artery. The energy supply of North America would be more secure and the strength of the economy of our largest trading partner would be increased.
Our supply of energy is important to us. Equally important to us is that the United States receives their supply of energy. Hon. members will recall how many Americans were out of jobs last winter and how seriously the slump in their economy affected Canada.
There is one other aspect. The pipeline group intends to employ thousands of people on the pipeline, something in the area of 5,000 or 6,000. This will be multiplied at least five times in other parts of Canada. That would be Hamilton, the maritimes, and as I told the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), they will probably eat a lot of fish in those pipeline camps.
I understand that another factor being considered is gas swaps. At the present time the important problem facing the United States is their short-term supply. The President of the United States has put into place a long term program but, as hon. members know, it takes a long lead time to bring these supplies on stream.
It is my understanding that affiliates of the Alaska-Yukon pipeline company are at the present time willing to deal with the United States on short-term supplies from western Canada. This is of considerable importance to the United States.
We have these additional supplies available. There appear to be various formulae to make possible their implementation. I urge the government to support these efforts and, wherever possible, to back those who are attempting to use these important levers to bring about acceptance by the United States of this particular route.
As I reflect on the figures of our own energy shortfalls in the eighties, I find them frightening. What is of even more concern is that the problem we have in energy is not truly an energy problem, but a political problem. It seems little short of incredible that Canada is programmed by this government in its studies to permit itself to lapse into heavy dependence on outside sources on the whims of foreign powers for its essential energy supply. It is all the more tragic when we realize that this potential energy is available in Canada through the various sources that we have.
There is the example of the northern regulations. This minister ought to be ashamed of himself. He has told this House and committee on more than two dozen occasions in the past six or eight months that these regulations would be available very soon. He said as recently as this past June that he would introduce them this session. We are well into the summer, and no regulations. This speaks very well for the concern the government has for the energy problem, and indeed the competence of the minister.
It is interesting that the government's program, the shortage and desperation in our actual supply situation, lead us very
much into the 1980's when we will be facing deficits which will not permit us to buy supplies. I wonder if the minister is aware of that.
Yesterday the Leader of the Opposition pointed out that studies by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and others clearly indicate that by the middle of the 1980's oil may very well not be available. This master plan, these studies, these words, all that we hear from this minister brings us to our maximum problem, our maximum shortages at the very time when world supplies will be phasing out and may very well be unavailable to us.
On the question of a northern pipeline, the government is obligated to come forward with some answers. It has had this problem for many years. The opportunity to build an oil line through Canada came at the time that Alaska oil was to be brought from Alaska. The government failed to react. It said no. It had an opportunity at that time to take steps to make possible the energy corridors, but it failed miserably. It is continuing to do so."]

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF PROPOSALS FOR NORTHERN GAS PIPELINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I indicated when the Chair gave me the floor last night, the construction of a pipeline assumes, for us Canadians, such importance as to be comparable with the great project achieved by our ancestors, namely the construction of the railway linking the east with the west, or the construction, more recently, of the St. Lawrence Seaway, as some of my colleagues pointed out yesterday during the debate, for it will contribute in a large measure to making Canada self-sufficient in matters of energy.
This special debate tops off several serious studies undertaken as early as in 1967, at which time the task force known as the North-West Project was set up whose main objectives were to make feasibility and engineering studies for the construction of a pipeline to transport natural gas from the Pointed Mountain in the Northwest Territories to the markets in the south. Some time later, in 1969, the Mackenzie Valley Pipeline Research Ltd. was created with a view to adding to the northwest project studies on a pipeline from Alaska and the Mackenzie Delta, as well as a link with existing pipelines. In 1970, other companies and task forces joined this core of researchers.
Following those important studies, groups of contractors applied to the National Energy Board for authorization to build a pipeline from Alaska and the Mackenzie delta to southern markets, by way of the Mackenzie Valley. In October 1976, Foothills Ltd. offered to build a pipeline for the transport of Alaska gas to American markets through the Yukon, British Columbia, Alberta, and Saskatchewan, a project whose approval was recommended by the National Energy Board last July. For us, eastern Canadians, this project represents many advantages well beyond the guarantee of an energy supply and assumes a very great importance. First, the implementation of this project will call for the participation of human and industrial resources in Canada and will obviously imply almost exclusive participation of the industry in Canada and naturally in the province of Quebec, more specifically for manufacturing the equipment needed to carry out the project such as compressors, generators, pumps, heavy machinery, air exchangers and so on. All this entails the creation of numerous jobs while at the same time boosting the processing industry in that province, not to mention the direct economic impact it will have all over the northwest region. Among the various benefits we are likely to get from that project, we must point out also, and they are not the least, the numerous permanent positions which will open up and which will be filled by natives. In short, Mr. Speaker, building a pipeline will represent another monument to the entrepreneurship of Canadians, a quality which is the pride of our country and which keeps on amazing the whole world. This great undertaking will be tailored to the size of our country.
In the few minutes available to me, how can I enumerate all the reasons that prompt us to build this pipeline now, whether we agree on the Foothills Yukon Ltd. or the Canadian Arctic
[Mr. Dupras.l
Gas proposals? The two are feasible without jeopardizing the environment and if there ever was a project as important as this one which has been considered as exhaustively as this pipeline, I cannot recall it, Mr. Speaker. This leads me to say that I find we have given a great deal more importance to environmental protection in the construction of a pipeline than we did to the opinion of Montrealers when time came to build Decarie Boulevard or the east-west expressway. Never was there such exhaustive consultation to make Canadians understand how important the building of such a project is. As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, the two are feasible without jeopardizing the environment and the self-reliance about which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) is talking in the foreword of the document entitled "An energy strategy for Canada", a document which the Leader of the Opposition does not seem to be aware of since he claimed that Canada has no energy policy. I suggest he should read it, for the minister stated we have in Canada the expertise, the material resources, the technology and the necessary energy resources we need to reduce our dependency on imported gas.
To achieve this, we shall have to reduce the rate of increase in our future energy needs, substitute more abundant types of energy resources for those which are less abundant, and speed up our search for oil and gas so as to transform our potential resources in proven resources and thus meet our needs. All these solutions are expensive, but we have no choice: we shall have to apply them fully, or else we shall be faced with energy shortages which will worsen our dependency on expensive and questionable oil imports, and even cut down on the available stocks in Canada. We are able to prevent the occurrence of those last two possibilities and we have to act accordingly. Those are, Mr. Speaker, the views of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
Furthermore, among the important reasons why we want to carry out this project now, there is also this opportunity we have to do so jointly and in sharing the costs with our neighbours south of the border, the Americans, with whom, it has to be admitted, we are already sharing the American continent as well as a continental defence system. We are also sharing many joint ventures, not to mention the professional hockey leagues, the major baseball leagues, Biscaine Boulevard in Miami and finally Cape Cod. Therefore we should not take offense at it, but feel a legitimate satisfaction at the fact that the solution to some of our energy problems could at the same time help resolve part of the serious difficulties our neighbours south of the border have faced these few last years.
Like the beneficial effects that the major gas discovery in the North Sea brought the British, something which is now being called the British economic miracle and which is the envy of the world of finance, even leading a Swiss banker to say that the British economic problems had been overcome through the valorization of the natural resources in the North Sea, the recovery, transformation and utilization of frontier natural gas represents in this country a capital event which in a few years will surely be called the economic event of the century. In the province of Quebec alone if consumption of
August 5, 1977

natural gas is to go from 6 per cent of total energy consumption to about 18 or 20 per cent one may extrapolate on the saving of oil which could result. That increased volume of gas consumption will help maintain the competitive quality of the industry of that province while also at the same time helping heat our residences and institutions.
One can also envisage the possibility of the day being delayed when the construction program for a nuclear reactor network will have to be implemented to provide the province with the energy supply it will need. It must also be anticipated that the construction of pipelines to serve the province and linking large cities which are not already supplied with natural gas will stir up construction activities leading to the establishment of infrastructures, Quebec City still being one of the rare large cities in North America not being yet supplied with that source of energy.
Mr. Speaker, the importance of that project for all Canadians was stressed by most hon. members who spoke before me in this debate, and it does seem that the most important question is not so much whether we are going to build the pipeline but rather when it will be built and what route it will follow. In light of the various reports that were produced by the Berger Commission, the National Energy Board as well as others who considered this important problem, the cabinet seems prepared to make a decision, and I am sure that decision and the challenge it will pose for all Canadians will be taken up by all Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my leader has set out very clearly the position of the official opposition with respect to a pipeline to bring gas from the Arctic. He has said, first of all, that we wholeheartedly support the principle of a gas pipeline, that the primary purpose of a pipeline is to deliver frontier gas to southern Canada, and that the secondary purpose of a pipeline is to deliver American gas to American consumers. He also said that based on available evidence-and I would like to emphasize the words "available evidence"-we support the Alcan route as recommended by the National Energy Board.
In order for a pipeline to be a reality, the approval of the United States will be required because at the moment there are not sufficient reserves of natural gas in the Delta to warrant a Canadian pipeline. The United States, of course, has the option of moving its gas down the El Paso route from Prudhoe Bay to Valdez, where it would be liquefied, put into LNG tankers and carried down the coast to California, or alternatively, as the President of the United States said in a speech a few days ago, through a new Panama Canal to the Gulf coast and eastern ports.
I read a report in yesterday's Globe and Mail that Basil Robinson, Canada's northern pipeline co-ordinator, and his team of negotiators received a "frosty" reception from their counterparts in Washington when they were down to work out the parameters of a Canada-U.S. agreement on an Alaska
Northern Gas Pipeline
Highway pipeline. I find this very hard to comprehend. Are we to understand that this was the first meeting held between Canada and the United States to consider pipeline proposals? That is, of course, other than the brief meeting which took place between President Carter and our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). I wonder, too, if the group of Canadian negotiators will include a representative of the government of the Yukon. After all, if we choose to build a pipeline along the Alcan route, it will affect the Yukon and it seens only logical, therefore, to include in the negotiations a representative of the Yukon, possibly an elected representative, or the Commissioner of the Yukon.
We face an impending world energy crisis, which makes it imperative for the United States to build a gas pipeline for moving its gas to the south, and also makes it imperative for Canada to build a pipeline for moving our gas to the south. Therefore, a Canada-U.S. line would be to our common advantage. Surely it would have made sense to hold a series of meetings during the past two or three years at which the two governments could have arrived at a tentative agreement or basic understanding, instead of waiting until the eleventh hour to begin the hard bargaining which will lead to an agreement.
I appreciate that applications for competing pipelines have been made in Canada and in the United States, that hearings must be held and decisions made; but would it not have been more reasonable to negotiate on the basis of all the options open to us? If that had happened, the government could have told the opposition parties in this debate, "We have worked out certain tentative proposals with the United States on the basis of existing options, and these are the alternatives. Let us now debate them on the basis of all the facts." It did not happen this way. We are now debating an issue on which we do not have all the relevant facts. The government is playing politics, hoping, 1 suspect, that the opposition will make a statement or statements based on inadequate evidence which the government can use at some future time to its political advantage. 1 note that yesterday the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) asked my leader the official opposition's position on the pipeline down the Mackenzie Valley, the CAGPL route. this government, without justification, led the people of the valley to believe there was no doubt the Mackenzie Valley pipeline would be built. The people in the valley built their hopes on it.
In Hay River, the headquarters of Northern Transportation Company Limited, a Crown corporation which carries freight by barge up and down the Mackenzie Valley and out to the islands in the Beaufort Sea, NTCL spent $20 million on barges and tugs in anticipation of activity to be created by construction of the pipeline. You will find the majority of this equipment either in drydock or tied up at wharves and not being used. In Norman Wells one will note that the government built some 20 houses, costing about $80,000 each, to accommodate the government employees it was anticipated would be needed in the area when the pipeline was built. Walking around Norman Wells you will come on a pile of 50 or 60 pieces of brand new furniture, chesterfields, chairs, and so on, still wrapped in cardboard. The furniture was destined for the houses under construction. Rain has fallen on it several times and I think it is now useless. Many thousands of dollars were wasted. As one resident said offhandedly to us, it will probably be thrown on the garbage dump.
One finds that Inuvik, at the suggestion of this government, developed an area and installed infrastructure for a new subdivision for homes for the people who would move into the town during the pipeline construction period and subsequently. This development cost the town several million dollars. We were told at Inuvik, as well, that DREE and the Industrial Development Bank had encouraged business to expand in anticipation of the pipeline being built. Now many businessmen are faced with large loan repayments which they are unable to meet. There are possibilities of shutdowns of businesses and even of bankruptcy. As I said earlier, there is a feeling of despair up and down the valley, despair caused by this government's lack of leadership, by lack of departmental co-ordination, by assumptions on the part of either ministers of the Crown or senior officials of their departments that, without doubt, a decision in favour of a Mackenzie Valley pipeline would be handed down.
I should be remiss in my duty if I did not put on record some of the feelings of many of the residents of the north with respect to the Berger commission hearings. We were told time and again that the report does not represent the true feelings of the majority of the native people but expresses the views, given through the mouths of native people appearing before the commission, of radical white advisers from the south. One name mentioned frequently was Mel Watkins, known to many as the former leader of the Waffle party. His views differ greatly from the views of the vast majority of Canadians and were so radical that the party to my left could not live with him.

1 am told for at least two years he was paid a salary of $45,000 a year by the Indian Brotherhood. We asked those who raised the issue why they did not appear before the
Berger commission to give their side of the story. Without exception, the answer given was that the majority of the groups which appeared before the commission were funded by the federal government. They were able to take the time to travel and had the funds to do so, whereas the people expressing their concern to us had businesses to look after and just did not have the time and the funds. Mr. Speaker, as I said earlier, I think it important to record in Hansard the views of those people.
In yesterday's mail, all members received a letter from John W. Steen, MLA for the western Arctic. That letter was dated July 14, 1977. Time will not permit me to read the whole letter into the record, but I would like to read three paragraphs. This is what Mr. Steen said:
I am a member of the Northwest Territories legislative assembly: although this assembly does not have the status of a provincial legislature, the members are no less the official representatives of our constitutents.
We, on the Northwest Territories legislative assembly are appalled at the tendency, however well intentioned, for southern Canadians to want to make our decisions for us. We are frustrated by our inability, due to our limited access to mass media, to make our true needs and desires known and understood nationally. Look at how much attention was given to Judge Berger's report and how little attention was paid to our assembly's assessment to the prospective Mackenzie Valley pipeline.
Once again, my plea to you is to let democracy work in the Northwest Territories-listen to the duly elected representatives of all peoples of the Northwest Territories. Do not force a moratorium down our throats.
If members will take the time to check the record, it will show that nine of the 15 elected members of the legislative assembly of the Northwest Territories are of native origin. 1 would suggest that these members do represent all the people in the territory. As representatives of all the people in the territory, the council must be actively involved not only in the negotiating area but in the final decision-making with respect to native land claims. The members of the legislative assembly recognize the right of the natives to a settlement of their land claims.
In the past four years I have made six trips into the Mackenzie Valley and have talked to a great many people. Not once did I talk to an individual who was opposed to a settlement. Without exception they said there should be a settlement and that the settlement must be just and equitable. However, they are opposed to a settlement along the lines of the Dene proposal. I would like to say, on my own behalf and on behalf of the official opposition, that we are opposed to any settlement along the lines proposed by the Dene. I can only classify their proposal as apartheid. It is interesting to note that the various organizations and groups throughout Canada who so vocally support the Dene proposal condemn even more vocally the apartheid policy of South Africa. How inconsistent can they be? In the debate yesterday, when the hon. member for Lambton Kent (Mr. Holmes) spoke he talked of the Dene proposal and apartheid and suggested that the government was sympathetic to it. The hon. minister for Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Allmand) then became quite agitated and I gathered from his remarks shouted across the floor of the House that he was denying it.

August 5, 1977

I would like to read into the record an excerpt from a letter dated June 28, 1977, written by the minister to David N. Searle, a member of the council of the Northwest Territories. The minister, referring to a meeting on April 19, 1977, in Yellowknife, said:
As I mentioned during our meeting, I reject the concept of an exclusively ethnic political unit, although I am not opposed to political units with native majorities, provided that minority political rights are protected.
I think this House and the people of Canada are entitled to an explanation of just what he means by that statement. Was he stating his own personal views, or government policy? The north, particularly the Northwest Territories, has suffered too long from the failure of the government to establish a northern policy. In the Diefenbaker years there was the vision of the north and the roads to resources policy. There was enthusiasm and anticipation on the part of all Canadians. It struck their imagination. But it was more than a vision. Projects were started. Some were completed, but unfortunately when the government changed, the north was forgotten. Prime Minister Pearson laughed at the Dempster Highway and said it was a road from igloo to igloo. Had that highway been built as planned by the Diefenbaker government, much of the equipment and supplies for Prudhoe Bay would have been carried over it. Think of what that would have done to Inuvik and Tuktoyaktuk.
This government has been a failure as far as the north is concerned. It has done everything it could to discourage development. It suspended the northern oil and gas regulations in 1970, and seven years later, despite repeated demands from oil companies and the official opposition, they still have not been drafted and promulgated. There has been a land freeze, preventing the development of some rich farmland and market gardening. There has been a freeze with respect to mineral exploration and development. The operation NCPC, a Crown corporation, has resulted in extremely high power rates to the residents of the north.
These are just a few examples of negligence of this government. They have failed to accept the fact that the territories at this point in time should have progressed to self-government by a phasing in of responsibility, that over the years the people of the north should have been consulted through their elected representatives to work out programs for the development of the north. The government may argue that settlement of land claims has held up development, but as someone mentioned yesterday in this debate, it was not until three years ago that the Prime Minister recognized the rights of the natives to a land settlement.
What is the future of the territories? How can the feeling of bewilderment and despair be overcome? I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that immediate steps must be taken to develop a policy that will stimulate oil and gas exploration in the Delta and the sedimentary basin of the valley. There must be a stimulus to mineral exploration and development. There must be a policy of hydro development tied into a Canadian power grid. There must be an opening up of farmland. There must be a good, hard look taken at logging in the southern part of the territo-
Northern Gas Pipeline
ries. There must be development of a transportation system in the north, in the broadest sense. The policies must not be developed solely in Ottawa, but primarily by the elected representatives of the people in the north with the co-operation of Ottawa. I see my time is up. I will close by saying that the situation in the valley is critical. I plead with this government to take immediate steps to work toward a solution to the problems.
