Mr. Speaker, I am indeed pleased to make a few comments on the motion before the House at this time. It is a very important decision that will affect not only the people living in the Yukon and Northwest Territories but all of the north. Indeed, the long-range effects of this major decision which I expect will be made within the next few weeks will affect all of Canada. I am willing to support this motion and amendment because of the quality of reports produced for the government in the past several months. I suggest that these be received by the government and given full consideration. However, I can only support this motion if I can see that the government truly and in good faith is willing to base its decision on the evidence and recommendations made public this past spring and summer.
If the government is using this motion to support a decision based on some other secret or confidential material it has prepared, and if in the next week or so we are treated to a decision based on information that is not now public, the cabinet will have made themselves, parliament and indeed everyone else involved look rather foolish. I certainly hope that does not happen. The decision that is to be made is a tall order for any group of people. I would like to help by reviewing the recommendations that have been made thus far. I would also like to add my own emphasis to these recommendations because the decision the government will be making in the near future is going to change my part of the country perhaps more than any other decision that may be made about the north in this decade.
I hope that all hon. members of the House will share my concern that the views of northern people are given just a little bit more of a fair hearing in deciding whether to build a gas pipeline down the Mackenzie Valley, along the Alcan route or whatever.
I should like to touch on some of the comments made by the major boards and commissions which have reported to the government on northern pipelines. By this I mean Mr. Justice Berger, the members of the National Energy Board, and the members of the Lysyk and Hill inquiries. First of all, I would again congratulate those people who worked so hard and conscientiously to prepare this material. To Judge Berger and the staff of the Berger inquiry, the people of the north, I believe, owe a debt that will be very difficult to repay. To the members and the staff of the other commissions and the NEB we owe a similar debt of gratitude for the full and fair way in which they have completed this work.

August 5, 1977
Northern Gas Pipeline
The manner in which these boards and commissions have included the public directly in the decision-making process is a welcome change from the way things have been done in the past, and I hope that these methods will set a precedent for the future. The way in which this material has been gathered shows the depth of feeling of Canadians generally about this major decision which affects the north. It shows that small groups and even individuals can have an influence on something as big and powerful as Canadian Arctic Gas. I believe that if it were not for the efforts of these boards and commissions, groups and individuals who devoted so much time and effort, we would now be watching Arctic Gas laying its pipeline along the Mackenzie Valley, which might have been a bad, even a dangerous, situation. These commissions and the people who appeared before them helped prevent that, and I certainly hope the government does not treat their efforts lightly.
In his report to this House, Mr. Justice Berger spoke of the social and economic cost of building a pipeline along the Mackenzie. Mr. Lysyk has this to say:
The main benefits from the pipeline will be concentrated outside the Yukon, largely south of the 49th parallel, whereas the most significant costs, in terms of both economic dislocation and social disruption, will be experienced in the Yukon.
The point is, Mr. Speaker, that when pipeliners go north to build they are not doing the northern people a favour. If the government decides to build a pipeline in either the Yukon or the Northwest Territories, it had better realize that it will do nothing but double or even triple our cost of living. There will be very few of us who will benefit from high wages; most of us will just have to pay. If the government does decide to go ahead, I plead with the government to have something a little more potent on hand than their useless wage controls.
I shall return to this question later as I would now like to go to the substance of the evidence. My reading of the four reports gives me the obvious general conclusion that there is a favourable reaction to the Foothills route, or, as it is more popularly known, the Alcan pipeline route, down the Alaska Highway. To my mind this is the best of a lot of bad choices and I would urge the government to consider it.
There are some loose ends though to be found in the fine print of these reports. These loose ends are not the fault of the commissions, but they are there and the government will have to do something about tying these loose ends together. In my view, one important loose end is the question of how pipeline development will mesh in with a settlement of land claims made by the native people of both the Yukon and the Northwest Territories.
It always strikes me as odd, Mr. Speaker, when you mention the words "northern development" to most people in the southern part of Canada they immediately think you are talking about a pipeline, or a hydroelectric project covering two billion acres, or anything that is really big and which costs more money than most of us can imagine. I will admit that some people in southern Canada do include, say, things such as forestry or fishing in their definition of "northern develop-

ment", but their number is few. Not that these things are not, strictly speaking, northern development; but I think these people miss the point that by far the most important kind of northern development-this is a point I have made several times not only in this House but elsewhere-would be a just settlement of native land claims both in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. Not only is settlement of a land claim economic development, in my humble opinion; it is also the means of social and political development for just over half, if not more, of the people of the north.
A just land claim settlement will set the background for most development, including construction of a pipeline in the future. A settlement would allow participation at several levels of government by native people through the economic activities that will shape the environment and the future of the people of the Yukon and Northwest Territories. I hope that as a result we will have some power, in terms of financial resources, to become participants in whatever economic development we choose, instead of being, as in the past, the victims of economic development which someone else far away from the scene chooses for us.
Perhaps more importantly, Mr. Speaker, a just land settlement will set the guidelines for how northern people will govern themselves and will relate to other levels of government both in the territories and in the rest of the country. A just land claims settlement would also influence the general land use patterns of the two territories. So far as this matter is concerned, the government does not have to listen only to me. Of the four reports that I have mentioned, three devote space to the topic of land claims. The fourth, the Hill report on environmental impact in the Yukon, did not include this topic within its scope.
Judge Berger has a lot to say in his report about land claims, and what he says is the best proof that he was able to understand the position taken by the native peoples at the hearings he conducted up and down the Mackenzie and indeed all across the country. At one in his report Judge Berger has this to say:
Euro-Canadian society has refused to take native culture seriously. European institutions, values and use of land were seen as the basis of culture. Native institutions, values and language were rejected, ignored or misunderstood and- given the native peoples use of the land-the Europeans had no difficulty in supposing that native people possessed no real culture at all.
Judge Berger goes on to say this:
Native culture is not static. The things the native people have said to this inquiry should not be regarded as a lament for a lost way of life, but as a plea for an opportunity to shape their own future, out of their own past. They are not seeking to entrench the past, but to build on it.
Judge Berger recommends that a period or ten years be set aside, and if this is done not only can a land claims settlement be reached but the settlement can be implemented before construction of a pipeline starts. He is adamant that no pipeline should be built before land claims are settled. He was speaking, of course, of conditions in the Northwest Territories.
Mr. Lysyk agreed that land claims in the Yukon must be settled before construction of a pipeline begins. He suggests that the period for implementation of the settlement be four
August 5, 1977

years. In the Yukon the native people have reached a kind of consensus. Based on that, they are willing to start negotiations for their claims. I am amazed that they have been able to complete this process in such a short time and with such apparent success.
In the Northwest Territories things are different. We have more than one culture, seven different languages and a different set of economic and political conditions. It will take much more time to work out a position that all the people in the Northwest Territories can feel comfortable with. This explains why the two territories need different time frames to complete a land claims settlement.
There is another important point which must be discussed, and I am referring to the other far-reaching effects of the building of a pipeline to the western Arctic, the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. I am speaking of the people who work in our mines, in our government departments, people who are employed by small business and people who own small businesses in the north. They will have to face a very big problem, and that is the effect of increased wages, high cost of living and the kinds of things which will come about as a result of high wages being paid to pipeline workers.
People in the mining business, small business, and so on, will have a difficult time contending with that. In the Yukon, these people make up by far the largest section of the work force. In the Northwest Territories, they are also a substantial percentage of the population. Presently these people, along with everyone else in the territories, face a cost of living far higher than anyone in the south. Also, it is harder to find a job in these territories than anywhere else in the country. I do not believe the building of any pipeline will help that.
In Alaska, during the construction period of their oil pipeline, the state was flooded with unemployed people from the lower 48 states, so much so that real unemployment in the state increased. There were more people without work during the construction period than before it started. This inflation will hit people who, even though their wages will no longer be controlled, I expect, will not be earning the pipeliner's dream wages. As I mentioned earlier, the miners will not, and the public service employees certainly will not. I could go on and on about this, but I believe there are a number of things that should be done before the construction of a pipeline commences. This is why I agree with the Lysyk recommendation for the Yukon, of a period of delay of four years, and the recommendation by Berger of ten years in the Northwest Territories.
Will the government make sure that Whitehorse and Yellowknife can afford to pay police officers, when the going rate for a night watchman is $4,000 or $5,000 a month on a pipeline-building project? Will they provide housing where a bunkroom full of people can cost $75 a week? Something like that happened along the route in Alaska during the building of the oil pipeline.
Northern Gas Pipeline
Another project that should be recommended before the building of any pipeline is the massive log housing program. There should also be job training. The Yukon people should be lobbying for the paving of the Alaska Highway, which would provide some jobs. The building of a massive log housing program in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories would assist the economy of those territories during the waiting period before settlement of land claims, and so on.
In conclusion, I should like to extend an invitation to all members of this House and all members of the other place to come to the north and see for themselves the kind of beauty and the kind of problems that have to be contended with up there. Perhaps if more members of this House and the other place had gone to visit the Northwest Territories in the past few years, the decision frontbenchers over there will have to make, or intend to make before too long, would have been a somewhat easier task.
Members opposite on the front benches have a big decision to make. They must assure a place for the rational development of gas, oil and other mineral wealth of the north. At the same time, they must assure a place in the development for the people of the north. They can turn it into a model of how men and women can live with respect for the land and the several cultures, or they can destroy the unique land and unique people. On behalf of the people of the Northwest Territories in particular, and all northerners, I say to the members in the front benches opposite, "Please be careful".

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF PROPOSALS FOR NORTHERN GAS PIPELINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I think that most Canadians are in favour of building an oil or gas pipeline, particularly because of the psychosis which has

August 5, 1977
Northern Gas Pipeline
been created for several years by the government and some so-called specialists who are trying to convince the public that there is a shortage of oil products. The government took every advantage of this and so has forced the Canadian people to accept the continuous increases in the gas and fuel prices. And today it says that Canada commits itself to build a pipeline and that a continuous supply is guaranteed for Canadians and it implies that this supply will cost less than the methods presently used.
It must be noted that the project guarantees at least a 25 year supply with the normal resources alone. This is what the studies indicate, which proves without any doubt that once again the so-called specialists, who try to make people believe there was a shortage of gas and oil products, were completely wrong.
To distract attention from the cost of installation, the debate has been centred on native rights and the environment. The Berger report speaks at length about this and even suggests a 10 year moratorium before starting to build a pipeline. I am wondering whether the experts have tried to make the population understand what such a project would cost-more than $10 billion according to pre-production estimates. Absolutely not. The experts talk about costs, but not more than is necessary. They talk about all sorts of aspects, but they forget to talk about money. The cost for the government and the companies involved has no importance or nearly none. When we consider what each investigation has cost-$48 million for the least expensive and more than $100 million for some others-we are talking about large expenditures. But this remains untold. What seems more important is to hide this figure of $10 billion to the population and to say that the cost is small and that it will contribute to stimulate the economy in an area of the country and that this investment will create employment.
What we of the Social Credit deplore is precisely this tendency of the government to refuse to reveal clearly and emphatically the cost of its projects for Canadians. However, we all know that Canadians will be the ones to pay for the project and that, according to present rates, interests of 9, 10 and even 12 per cent will have to be paid on these $10 billion. However, this is not mentioned. Whether the investment is made by private companies or jointly with the government, it still remains that Canadians will pay the cost.
The motion we are discussing today attempts to emphasize the agreement of all parties to the building of a pipeline, which forces us to set certain priorities, namely the significance of and need for such a project, and especially its impact.
Clearly there is an all-important factor, capacity for a , nation to be self-sufficient. It is important for a country like Canada to be independent, not to depend on foreign countries. This one reason alone gives us the right to support the construction of a pipeline that would obviously allow us to use our own resources.

We feel that this one reason is ample justification for supporting the project, with the provisos stated earlier and others I shall refer to later.
My second question concerns the need for a pipeline. Is it important for Canada's development, is it absolutely necessary? This may be the key to the whole problem. Although the proposed pipeline now appears to be a necessity of some sort, we wonder whether it will still be four or ten years from now.
Since all reports agree on a four- to ten-year postponement, we can justifiably ask ourselves whether, during that period, the government would not be better advised to spend the pipeline's estimated cost on researching other forms of energy that would not harm the environment. The proposed delays are based on environment and native sociology reasons. Every report refers to the need for postponing construction to obtain a better knowledge of the environment. Would it not be better if the government looked for other sources of energy? How far down the road can we expect that solar energy will be tapped, that tide or wind energy will be in general use and, in a still more technologically advanced area, that the earth's magnetic energy will be developed? This is the question I am pondering. Why not spend the same amount of money on developing other forms of energy? Will the pipeline project seriously jeopardize research in other fields? Why did the studies not order comparative analyses of the development of other resources and that of oil and gas transportation?
To my mind, a government concerned with the common good would have, right from the start, ordered such a report before looking into which route would be the best for building a 20- or 48-inch pipeline. I agree with the idea of a pipeline, but I am still reticent about its value in twenty years from now, especially knowing that Canadians, in 100 years from now, will still be paying for the cost of the project which will probably have been profitable for barely ten years. Still, I am quite willing to try to find out what its consequences will be. But, once again, I have to refer to all those studies which, without a single exception, point out the ecological dangers while at the same time advising us that it is impossible to evaluate its repercussions, at least the most important, namely the respect of our aboriginals and the environment. In that respect alone, we are floundering in strange waters, at the risk of making the same error as our ancestors who, in the name of industrialization, did not evaluate the destruction of the environment, the pollution of our rivers by industrial waste, and so many other consequences we are now up against.
Nevertheless, I must congratulate those responsible for the reports for at least thinking about the future impact of such a project. And for that I endorse the suggestion, but as I mentioned my support remains conditional on the answers that will be provided by the further inquiries, if any, and the attitude of the government. For the economic good of the country we certainly support the proposed pipeline but for the good of Canadians we believe that the government would be more respectful of reality if it tried just as much to develop the other sources of energy that seem to me to be less risky for the environment.
August 5, 1977

In conclusion, I want to mention that whatever project the government accepts, its financing will be done under the present economic and monetary policy based on the conventional methods of the old parties; whatever the project approved by government, it will force the people to pay ten times the actual value of the project, if it is a gas pipeline it will force the people to pay ten times the actual cost of the pipeline with only one pipeline being built. As usual, Canadians will pay for one pipeline and ten of them to financiers. Unfortunately, that is the normal practice of a government that remained hooked on the economic residues of the eighteenth century. I am much more looking forward to a debate on the changing of that economic policy than a proposed pipeline such as the one that is now before us.
On the whole, those are the remarks I wanted to make and I want to repeat that, unfortunately, whatever the attitude of this government on whether or not to approve a pipeline, once again through interests or the multiplication of interests Canadians will have to pay the cost of such a facility not one time but ten times over as happens with all government investments. I think that in the case of a project which initially should cost an estimated $10 billion-if one takes the example of James Bay the estimates were about 80 per cent below actual cost-one realizes that when such a project gets going we will no longer be talking about $10 billion but a much more considerable figure. What is unfortunate in all this is that the government does not want to take into consideration the suggestions made by the Social Credit Party of Canada, but projects of such magnitude as this should, if the government gets directly involved, be financed by interest free loans. So, once again, the ideas put forward with respect to a gas pipeline are certainly a contribution to the Canadian economy but at the same time it is also a deficit, an unthinkable debt to put on the backs of Canadians.
Mir. Frank Maine (Wellington): Mr. Speaker, with regard to the decision on whether or not to build the northern pipeline, there are five major questions which must be addressed and answered.
The first question is that of need. Do we need the energy, do we need the gas in the north to bring down to southern markets?
The second question relates to the science and technology involved in building a pipeline. Do we have the necessary science and technology to construct a pipeline adequately and safely to transport the natural gas?
The third question involves the environment. Can a pipeline be built with adequate safeguards to the environment so that the ecological price will not be devastating?
The fourth major question is that of the native land claims. Can we resolve these satisfactorily to give justice and equity to the people involved?
Northern Gas Pipeline
The fifth and most important question over-all because it affects the previous four questions is that of economics. Can we satisfy the four earlier requirements and reach an economically viable solution? I would like to deal with each of these questions in some detail.
The first and most important question is that of need. Do we need the energy; do we need the natural gas to construct a pipeline to bring it down from the north? I heard no evidence to the contrary expressed in the House yesterday or today that both the United States and Canada have a need for more energy, and, in particular, for more natural gas. The question is not if, but when. Here we come to the first major difference between the two needs, that of the United States and that of Canada. The U.S. need is immediate. If anything, it is more than immediate. They needed gas last year, as was evident from the crisis which occurred in the U.S. last winter at which time we were able to assist them in solving some of the major problems they faced. Canada's need is not immediate. Right now we have adequate gas-if anything, we have a small surplus of gas. As can be projected from the studies that have been tabled, our real need will be in the early 1980's, assuming the continuation of past practices.
There are some options which could be exercised to change that situation quite significantly. I will come back to the question of need and some of its implications after I have addressed the other four major questions. In the area of science and technology, judging from the reports we have seen, there is no question that we have an adequate data base to answer the questions involved. There is still some work to be done, especially in the area of engineering, as has been brought to light recently with respect to the proposed Alcan line, both with the Dawson Bulge and the Dempster Lateral. The engineering studies have not been completed and will have to be finalized before a decision can be reached.
The same situation exists with regard to the environmental question. There is an indication that we can answer the questions involved, that we can satisfactorily protect our environment in the future, but we have not yet completed the work that must be done. The second phase of the Lysyk inquiry should be undertaken as soon as possible to finalize the questions that have not yet been answered adequately, and that will take some time. But there is no indication at this stage that we cannot solve the environmental questions within the economic constraints.
The fourth question, that of the native land claims settlement, and the related socio-economic effects of the pipeline on the natives. Again, both the Berger and Lysyk inquiries addressed these questions in some detail. I fully agree that these questions should be given a high priority and that all attempts should be made to answer them before the construction of the pipeline. Again, we have to maintain an adequate awareness of the economic constraints in this question. There is not an unlimited amount of money to spend.
This brings me to the fifth point to be addressed, that of economics. It depends on the settlement of the above questions,

August 5, 1977
Northern Gas Pipeline
but it is also guided by the alternative solutions to bringing natural gas from the north.
Because of the different needs of Canada and the United States several alternatives are open to us. I should like to illustrate briefly the four options that I consider to be viable options in attempting to satisfy our energy needs by way of satisfactory transportation. First there is the Alcan route by itself. By this I mean a pipeline from Prudhoe Bay via Fairbanks and Whitehorse down to British Columbia and Alberta with no side connections, strictly a natural gas pipeline to transport gas from Prudhoe Bay south to the markets in the United States.
The second option is the Alcan route with the Dempster Lateral, with or without the Dawson Bulge. Again there are several questions to be answered in that option: the economics of the change, the engineering studies that have not yet been done, and the environmental questions.
The third option is one which I think defines the economic limitations, that is, the El Paso line which takes the natural gas from the northern slope in Alaska by pipeline to Valdez on the southern Alaskan coast and then by liquefied natural gas (LNG) tanker to the southern 48 states.
There is a fourth alternative to consider so far as Canadian needs are concerned, and that is the Polar Gas option whereby instead of taking U.S. gas to U.S. markets, as the El Paso route does, we will take Canadian gas from the Arctic islands to Canadian markets via liquefied natural gas tankers. I would like to emphasize that that option has not been outlined in this debate so far but it is a very viable option and it satisfies the very pertinent questions that are raised.
As I mentioned earlier, our needs for gas are not immediate and if we are looking primarily at satisfying our markets so far as natural gas is concerned, we do not have the same time pressure as do the Americans. Therefore, in our time frame, if for one reason or another the Dempster Lateral is not a viable alternative, the Polar Gas LNG tanker route is a viable solution to consider. We are not talking about having to build a pipeline. We have to liquefy the natural gas in the Arctic islands after collecting it, and then ship it by LNG tanker through the Northwest Passage down to the east coast. There are many attractive features about this option, and I submit that this is a very real option which should be considered in our negotiations with the United States.
This brings me to the question of the negotiations with the United States and the very important variables Canada should consider in these negotiations. Time is a very pressing question as far as the need for gas by the Americans is concerned. The question of the swapping of natural gas to buy more time is another question. Right now Canada has an excess, and when I talk about swapping I am talking about volume for volume at the same price. In other words, if we give them some of our gas now at whatever the going price, that gas should be replaced at the same price sometime in the future with American gas from the Arctic slope.

The details of the route are also further negotiating points. These details have been suggested by a variety of sources. The National Energy Board has brought in some new variations. There have been other reports which have raised other questions as to route options which have not been fully discussed or decided upon. Another negotiating point is the whole question of native land claims. There has been debate already on the American position as to whether the pipeline treaty recently signed by Canada and the United States prohibits a $200 million pay-out which has been recommended in the Lysyk report and in other reports.
In the Canadian context I think it would only be fair to keep in mind the James Bay settlement. It would be appropriate to use that settlement in the Yukon. I think the settlement with the natives in the Yukon should not be any lesser a settlement than that arrived at with the Indians in the James Bay area. Conversely, we cannot have a settlement in the Yukon which is better than that at James Bay, for equality reasons and for economic reasons in competition with the El Paso option.
Then there are further negotiating points to consider. With regard to the option of the Dempster Lateral, environmental and engineering studies should be started as soon as possible. If that option is the one to be utilized, there is the whole question of Canadian content as well as the question of financing. With Canadian participation and with Canadian gas going to Canadian markets from Canadian fields it is quite different from the Alcan route without the Dempster Lateral, in which case we are talking only about U.S. gas going to U.S. markets. In that case I think there is no justification whatsoever for any dependence on Canadian financing for that option at all. These are negotiating points we should be very aware of and use very wisely and strongly.
The question of science and technology is another important negotiating point. There should be Canadian content not only in the materials and labour for the pipeline but also in the engineering design. We have a pretty lousy deal in the Cana-da-U.S. auto pact. Canada has not benefitted at all with regard to science and technology in the auto pact. All research and development and all engineering design is done in Detroit. In this regard Canada does not participate independently in the automotive industry. Canada is completely dependent on the United States, and Canada has only manufacturing facilities. I feel that is a totally untenable situation. We should learn from that mistake and not make it again with any pipeline in the north. We should be involved not only in materials and labour but also in engineering design and development capability. That would benefit us in the future for future pipelines which will undoubtedly be built.
I therefore recommend, as other parties have done, that Canada proceed with negotiations with the United States, that there be given approval in principle to build a northern pipeline, but let it be contingent on a satisfactory resolution of several of the details I have mentioned. After the negotiations have resulted in mutual satisfaction, legislation should be introduced into the Canadian Parliament which would provide the details of the route and other pertinent aspects which will
August 5, 1977

have been negotiated so that parliament can debate this important and massive project and make a final decision in full view of the Canadian public so that there can be full participation of all the people in the country.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Maine). I can only say that if the excellent speech he made had been made by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen), or if the minister's speech had been half as good, the government would have had something of which to be proud.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF PROPOSALS FOR NORTHERN GAS PIPELINE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF PROPOSALS FOR NORTHERN GAS PIPELINE
speechtext:
Many points were raised by the hon. member for Wellington, but I would like to make one observation on one specific point. He spoke about the possibility of the alternative of moving gas from northern regions by ship, or by what I call the eastern route. I agree that it is a possible and viable alternative, but it is deplorable that the government pays lip service to our shipbuilding industry and to the reconstitution of our merchant marine but does absolutely nothing to encourage an expertise in one area of merchant marine in which Canada should be expert, and that is the type of navigation and transportation the hon. member for Wellington has just outlined so ably.
The motion which is the subject matter of this debate asks that this House recognize four issues surrounding the question of northern gas pipelines. These are social, economic, environmental and energy issues. Much could be said about each, but time limitations permit me to deal with only one of these, that being the environment.
I start with the proposition-which is likely self-evident- that a pipeline does nothing to enhance our Canadian environment. Therefore the challenge is to minimize the impact this huge project would have on the ecology of our far north. Probably the greatest risk would be experienced during the construction period, but I would like to remind the House that the potential for an adverse impact upon the environment continues during the time which might be called the withdrawal from construction period and during the third stage, which is the continuing period of pipeline operation.
For those who might question the importance of these latter two stages I need only point out the problems which have been experienced in Alaska with the recently completed Alyeska oil pipeline. In the few short weeks since the completion of that line there have been serious problems of technical faults, operation error, waste disposal, and suspected sabotage. The risks arising from these problems affect not only the environment but may also have a serious social and economic impact as well as bring about an interruption of energy supply.
I remind the government, therefore, that the need for control and precautionary measures does not terminate with the end of construction. I further remind the government that in the event of construction of a pipeline the government will have no excuse whatsoever for not having in place adequate
Northern Gas Pipeline
controls for the withdrawal from construction and operation periods. This requires particular emphasis because this is a government which has had a long and unhappy history of permitting dangerous situations to develop and then reacting to them without adequate studies and preparation, and nowhere has this been more obvious than within the Department of the Environment.
As an example we need only look to the Beaufort Sea, an area which experienced what could only be called a crash study on environmental impact, followed by a hope and pray period, and then followed by the granting of drilling permits with conditions which possibly are too stringent and possibly are too lenient. Who knows? Had the Department of the Environment spent a comparable amount of effort and resources in becoming scientifically excellent in its weather and ice predictions, we could likely have been in a much more flexible and confident position when drilling permits were issued. Therefore, with regard to the period following construction of a pipeline I ask that the government adopt what is, for it, a unique course of action; and that is planning instead of reacting.
However, the immediate concern is the construction period, in the event the government should give its approval. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) has said that we approve in principle the Alcan route on the basis of available information. There is a deplorable and inexcusable lack of environmental information on the Alcan proposal, and I assure this House that I do not seize upon this lack of information as an excuse for opposing construction of a pipeline. I regard it as a missing tool essential to the planning and construction of a pipeline which is as compatible with our environmental concerns as is possible.
There are two basic sources of the necessary environmental data. The first of these sources is government, principally through its Department of Fisheries and the Environment, the second, of course, is the private sector and, in the case of a pipeline, one expects to receive substantial data from the company or group of companies that proposes and seeks government approval for the construction.
Such was certainly the case with regard to the proponents of the Mackenzie Valley route who commissioned and filed at least 41 volumes of biological reports. I do not suggest that the proponents of the Alcan route have done nothing in this regard, because they have filed significant and helpful material including, incidentally, an initial environmental evaluation prepared by the Alaska highway pipeline panel which was sponsored by Foothills Pipe Lines Limited. To suggest, however, that we have received anything more than very preliminary environmental information would simply not be in accordance with the facts. I suggest that it is the direct responsibility of the pipeline proponents to bear the cost of supplying all necessary environmental data. Second, I believe, on the basis of information received from these companies, that they acknowledge this responsibility and are willing to assume it.

August 5, 1977
Northern Gas Pipeline
The other source of environmental information, as I have mentioned, is government itself. Much baseline data has been accumulated over the years by various government departments or agencies. Other data may be gathered more effectively and efficiently by government than by the private sector proponent. Recognizing that it is the proponent's responsibility to prepare the required reports, it is government's responsibility to supply any existing data to the proponent. Where government is better able to gather additional data, it is its responsibility to do so. If this demands accelerated or additional programs resulting in unbudgeted costs, it is the proponent and not the taxpayer who should likely pay these costs.
Finally, the government is responsible for evaluating the proponent's reports and, as a result, prescribing the regulations and conditions attaching to any approval for pipeline construction.
With regard to the Alcan proposal, the principal environmental report is that of the environmental assessment panel dated July 27, 1977, and entitled "Alaska Highway Pipeline". This report has come to be called the Hill report because the distinguished chairman of the panel was Dr. Harry M. Hill of the Department of the Environment.
On August 30, 1976, Foothills made its application for a certificate of public convenience and necessity to the National Energy Board. On the same day, August 30, 1976, it applied to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Allmand) for a right-of-way to build its pipeline through part of the Yukon. At this point it was obvious that this proposal required the application of the government's environmental assessment and review process, commonly called EARP. This was obvious on August 30, 1976, first because a significant part of the project would pass through federally administered lands and, second, because the project had the potential for significant environmental impact. Despite this it took almost seven months, until March 21, 1977, before the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development referred the matter to his colleague, the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc), for an assessment of the environmental impact. This seven month delay is not only unexplained; in my party's view it is inexcusable and unacceptable.
Hon. members should realize that the normal EARP procedure is for the EARP panel to issue guidelines under which the proponent prepares an environmental impact statement. The EARP panel then does the technical review of the report and makes its recommendations to the minister. With regard to the Foothills proposal, the request for a review was not even made until seven months after the Foothills application, which certainly indicated that the government was not even treating the application seriously at the time.
Following receipt of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development's application for a review, the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment then took almost another month, until April 19, 1977, before he formed a panel, or at least appointed Dr. Hill as chairman. In my view that was a reasonable time span in which to establish an environmental assessment review panel. He then proceeded to give the panel
[Mr. Jarvis.l
until August 1 to prepare its report, less than three and a half months. Dr. Hill, in the introduction to his report, points out at page 3:
The short lead time available made a normal environmental assessment of the project impossible at this time.
He then goes on to say at page 4:
The requirement for the environmental assessment panel to file an interim report by August 1, 1977 necessitated a significant departure from procedures normally followed in panel operations.
As if the situation faced by Dr. Hill and his colleagues on the panel were not difficult enough, they were asked subsequently to consider alternate Yukon routes, plus consideration of the Dempster Lateral, plus a comparison of the environmental impact between the Mackenzie Valley and Alaska highway routes. In my view this was an impossible task. I in no way question the ability or integrity of the Hill panel; on the other hand, I point out that their report is printed testimony to the frustration of attempting to do too much too late. Therefore when we in this party indicate that our support for the Alcan route is based on available information, we emphasize that the Hill report points out quite accurately, the serious lack of environmental information. My approach to this report is to use it not as an environmental assessment but as a catalogue of problem areas which must be faced immediately, effectively and efficiently.
I repeat that 1 do not search for environmental problems to find an excuse for delaying or opposing important decisions but rather to ensure that the implementation of these decisions may be accomplished with the minimum of adverse impact to the Canadian environment.
Let me quickly run through the Hill report, with particular emphasis on the deficiency of information which it outlines. I deal first with Chapter III, to do with physical and engineering concerns. With respect to geotechnical aspects, mainly permafrost and seismic activity, the panel devotes almost a full page to information deficiencies, including emphasis on a limited data base. With regard to water crossings, there is an inadequacy of biologic, hydrologic and soils data. Concerning erosion control the panel says that stabilization techniques are not sufficiently developed. Insufficient information is available to predict the impact of various facilities and structures.
According to chapter IV dealing with biological concerns, there is insufficient knowledge of life histories and exploitation rate of fish, and major deficiencies exist in the knowledge of wildlife and waterfowl populations. In chapter V on unique and sensitive areas, the panel says we require detailed environmental assessments of four specified geographic areas. According to chapter VI on aesthetics and recreation, a systematic assessment of probable aesthetic impact is required. Chapter VII deals with associated developments. The panel was not convinced that sufficient planning had been done to minimize the impact of such projects as highways and hydroelectric construction. Chapter VIII deals with other possible pipeline routes. In addition to the Alaska highway route, the panel considered alternates along the Klondike highway and Tintina Trench, but they concluded that insufficient data was available
August 5, 1977

to draw any definite conclusion from a comparison of alternate routes in the southern Yukon.
To put all of this in perspective, Mr. Speaker, we must realize that the Hill report concludes that the pipeline can be constructed and operated in an environmentally acceptable manner, provided three conditions are met: first, that the environmental planning is properly carried out; second, that we can avoid or solve the problems in unique and sensitive geographic areas; and third, that environmental problems associated with permafrost areas can be overcome.
Similarly, there is nothing in the report to indicate that these three conditions cannot be met within the permissible time frame between now and the commencement of construction. Finally, the panel concluded that the Alcan route is environmentally preferable to a Mackenzie Valley route.
Therefore, in connection with Canadian accommodation to permit the United States to move its natural gas through our territory to U.S. consumers, if the government were to approve in principle the Alcan route, it seems self-evident that the normal EARP procedures should be expedited so that we might benefit from a proper and meaningful environmental assessment review, having confidence that such review could be completed in a reasonable time. This is consistent with the commitment made by the Minister of the Environment on April 19, 1977, when he first established the Hill panel. At that time the minister said:
... If the Alaska highway pipeline project is still a contender after decisions have been made in the competing proposals, the normal panel procedure would then be followed.
It is essential that the minister, given the situation I have mentioned, reaffirm this commitment at the earliest possible date.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, this all relates to the secondary purpose of this whole exercise, that of moving U.S. gas to U.S. markets. The primary objective has for years been the transportation of Canadian natural gas to Canadian markets. It was this objective which initiated all of the various studies and applications and which must remain our principal concern. The shift in emphasis from the Mackenzie route to the Alcan route does nothing to mitigate this concern about Canadian resources destined for Canadian consumers.
There are a number of possibilities in terms of moving this gas. Much has been said during this debate about the Dempster Lateral to connect with the Alcan line. This would permit Mackenzie Delta and Beaufort Sea gas to be transported via this spur to connect with the main Unites States line near Dawson. There are other alternatives as well. The important point is this-if a real possibility, not probability, but real possibility, exists that a certain route or routes may be used for transporting this gas, the time to commence the environmental assessment review process is now. It will be inexcusable for the Minister of the Environment to wait, as has been the govern-
Northern Gas Pipeline
ment's policy, until a situation develops when we can do little more than react because time limitations do not permit us to do the proper planning.
I put the minister on notice that we in this party and, I believe, Canadians everywhere, will not permit him and the government to ignore their obligation to our country to provide an environmental process in keeping with the importance of our trusteeship for our Canadian environment.
In chapter VIII of his report Dr. Hill deals with the Dempster Lateral and points out that three to five years would be required for a program to evaluate potential environmental impacts and mitigative measures. The report lists point after point wherein adequate information is lacking. The report goes on to conclude that, if a decision is made to continue planning for the transportation of Alaska gas through the southern Yukon, an environmental impact assessment of the construction and operation of the Dempster Highway be undertaken immediately.
The panel points out that the study of the highway itself is a prerequisite to the assessment for the possible pipeline. It is to this recommendation that the minister must respond, and I point out to him that this conclusion of his own officials is not based on the probability of moving Canadian gas along this route.
Dr. Hill and his colleagues are saying, in the clearest terms, that continued planning to construct the line to move United States gas through the southern Yukon is reason enough for us to prepare now our environmental assessment of the Dempster Lateral.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote from the report of the Alaska Highway pipeline panel which, as you know, was a committee of distinguished Canadians sponsored by Foothills Pipe Lines Ltd. and whose initial environmental evaluation I found most helpful and informative. This group had this to say:
If the government is not ready to control the pipeline, the pipeline should not be built.
In terms of environmental concerns we on this side expect that the first evidence of government control would be the assumption and discharge of government responsibility. Regretfully, little evidence of this is available to date. To permit seven months to go by before application for creation of the EARP panel is evidence only of the government's wish to avoid its responsibility.
Perhaps a positive response to the Hill report, on behalf of the Minister of the Environment, might be the first small step toward the recognition of its responsibility and assumption of control that Canadians deserve to expect from their government.

As a British Columbian I also support the construction of the Alcan Pipeline if the Canadian government is able through negotiations to arrive at a satisfactory agreement with the United States, satisfactory to Canada and at the

same time assisting our neighbour to the south, the United States of America, at a time when I consider their need to be critical for natural gas.
The Canadian government will indeed be facing a challenge because the United States will be tough bargainers. This is in no way depreciating the United States. However, at all times it must be remembered that the Alcan Pipeline will be transporting American gas to American consumers through Canada, and although economically Canada will gain certain advantages, Canada will also incur social disadvantages.
In my opinion Canada must deal from a position of strength, taking into consideration the Americans' need for natural gas, a strength based on our desire to assist this nation solve its critical gas shortage, a strength based on principles of fairness and equity to both Canada and the United States.
In order to show our realization of the critical need the United States has for natural gas in the northern tier, we as Canadians should be willing to lift export restrictions on Alberta natural gas in conjunction with the Alberta government before next winter, if an agreement in principle can be reached regarding pipeline construction, and to have the gas replaced in the future when Prudhoe Bay gas begins flowing through the Alcan pipeline. This would assist independent producers in Alberta, assist rectify our balance of payments deficit, and also indicate our awareness of the critical need facing the United States for natural gas.
I would also recommend to the cabinet that the price be set at current export gas rates, and that Canada have the option to purchase the same quantity exported, an option that may not be required if further significant natural gas finds are made at some subsequent date.
Negotiations with the United States must clearly give absolute sovereignty over choice of route, and timetable to the people of Canada. Needless to say that project and construction management, labour content, financing and construction itself must be Canadian in content. One problem that has already surfaced is that of shortages in certain skilled professions. I would recommend that with the three to four year lead time an assessment be made of labour requirements, and where shortages exist of skilled labour such as welders, pipefitters, and so forth, provincial and union consultation take place through Manpower in order that Canadians are put to work. It would be a shame if we had to import construction workers from other parts of the world at a time when we in Canada have significantly high unemployment.
At the present time Foothills is well aware that imported workers will be required if no concerted effort is made to train and upgrade Canadians. We are talking of a significant labour force for the construction of the Alcan pipeline. At peak construction period the total manpower requirements are expected to reach 7,800.
It would be the height of absurdity if unemployed Canadians did not work during the pipeline construction because the skills are not there. We have a lead in period of time where there could be consultation between the federal government,

provincial governments, labour, the unions and so on in order to get these people upgraded, not only for pipeline construction but past the completion of the pipeline. I hope the government will be cognizant of the fact that we have an opportunity that may not come our way again. We must upgrade the skills of Canadians in order that the construction of the line will be done for Canadians by Canadians.
We are all aware that the United States has an alternative to the building of a pipeline in Canada. El Paso has proposed the building of a pipeline from Prudhoe Bay to Valdez and then trans-shipping liquefied natural gas to California. As a member from British Columbia, I am totally opposed to any increase in tanker traffic of any size, form or shape. 1 only wish that we had television in the House today, Mr. Speaker, because I would jump and dance around a bit to make sure that this point is made. I think that even my friends in the Conservative party from British Columbia will agree with me on this issue. We do not agree with the Conservative party in British Columbia on very much, but I think that even they would agree, indeed any Conservative, Liberal, NDP-er or Social Crediter, that we in British Columbia are opposed to tanker traffic off our west coast. I do not think it would be unfair to say that there is no one issue in British Columbia today on which the people are so totally united. We are well aware of what will happen, that it is only a question of time, and this explains why we do not want any tanker traffic.
I would also ask the cabinet, when it sits down with United States negotiators to discuss the problems associated with Cherry Point, which is in the state of Washington-

Mr. Speaker, it is with a feeling of some sadness that I participate in this debate. It is almost exactly 20 years ago when, as the first act of the Diefenbaker administration, we proposed a royal commission on energy to look into the terrible things which had happened to Canada in the case of Westcoast Transmission in 1954 and in the case of TransCanada PipeLines in 1956. I remember the horrible mistakes which were made during that whole period, and I now see the government repeating those mistakes, probably unwittingly, today.
Even more than the feeling of sadness which I have over the ignorance of the government regarding the mistakes we have made in the past is the feeling of personal sadness that I have over the several thousand people who lived in the Yukon and Northwest Territories when, as a southern government, we built schools all through the settlements of the Yukon, and in the Northwest Territories in the larger settlements, and asked the native people to give up their young and send them to these schools. We flew them into schools at Fort Smith, Yellowknife and Inuvik and flew them back for their holidays. The appeal that we made to their parents was very simple, and at that time honest and sincere: if you give us your children-because we know there is no future on the land for them,-and we educate them in the white man's ways, there will be a job for them when they graduate.
Those schools were built mostly during the period from 1957 to 1963. The students who came into those schools in the early days in Fort Smith, Yellowknife, Inuvik, and up as far as Old Crow, have graduated; but they are still awaiting the development that was promised. They were told that if they left their homes, their loved ones, and came to these boarding schools for eight to ten months of the year we would provide work for them.
When the government changed in 1963, all development stopped in the north. Regulations that we had to induce the oil and gas industries to explore and expand were suspended in 1970 and are still not in effect. The dream we had in 1957 was that we knew by 1980 North America would be short of energy and minerals. We also knew that it would take 20 years to lead time to get into the north and make access to these resources available to the whole world, and not only North America. Part of that equation was the human factor. We promised a future to these young Indians and Eskimos, and we have failed in that pledge which was made in good faith 20 years ago, because we sit opposite a government that is only concerned with public relations or, as they call it, communications-anything to keep in the headlines. It has ignored

August 5, 1977
Northern Gas Pipeline
Canadian interests from first to last. If anyone reads the history of our country from 1939 to 1957, he will see that the history was the same. The leading historian of our nation called it "the forked road". We took the wrong fork in the road.
I say these remarks in introduction because I want to get to the part of this problem that offers opportunity, which is not all lost. I should have liked to hear in this debate how this whole energy development on the North American continent plays an active part in the total development of the world. With a world begging for development and begging for higher standards of living, we stand in our places talking about trivialities. I am sorry the hon. member for Edmonton-Strath-cona (Mr. Roche) could not get his speech in, because he would have dealt with that subject.
We have learned lesson after lesson over the last 30 or 40 years. One thing I have noticed is that they are orientated the wrong way and they are costly. When we set up the National Energy Board Act, we set up hearings for specific purposes. Other functions have been added since, such as native rights and the environment. All these things were not connected and moving completely without concern for the other factor. As the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) said in opening up the debate yesterday, we are debating something and we have not got the information. Everyone is recommending the Dempster route because no one has studied it. The only ones they do not recommend are the ones they have studied. Partially these hearings are to blame.
Business has learned that before you start on a big project you must have a conceptual hearing to look at the entire strategy, so that every component part has a place in this strategy. From this you build your critical path so that each person knows what he has to do and the time he has to do it in. Over the last seven years the first lesson we have learned is that the whole concept of the technique of hearings in these cases should be changed. If we have an industrial or a development strategy, it should be put down as a concept, and around that concept you begin to build what you have to do.
The next thing is this question of socio-economic responsibility. I heard the Leader of the Opposition say yesterday that he wanted one of the conditions to be that private companies would have some share in the economic and social responsibility of a major construction project.
This gas has nothing to do with Canada, except for the odd little bit which will spurt up alongside the pipeline. This is American gas going from one American state to another American state. We must lay down the conditions under which they build through our country. It is as simple as that. This should apply to domestic enterprises as well. What share is to be borne by all the people of Canada of the socio-economic costs? What share is to be borne by the private entrepreneur?
Another significant lesson is transportation. Twenty years ago I stood in this House to say that the major priority was transportation to open up the north. That is still the major priority. Here we are 20 years later, after having started a program of opening up the north, and we still have not got one

major land route to the Arctic. We got up 80 miles north of the starting place in the Yukon. We got to Yellowknife, and stopped when the government changed in 1963. We should have a transportation corridor in place including a railway, the road, and the pipeline. All this spending of money locating routes has to stop. It is just not allowable up there in the north.
I could list case after case where we have completely failed as Canadians to fight for Canadian interests. Even Berger, duped as he was by the doctrines and rhetoric of the Waffle or the anti-Americans, did not say there should not be a pipeline on the Mackenzie. He knows there has to be one. He simply said to postpone it ten years to give native people a longer time to complete their bargaining for native rights; but that turned out to be the death knell for the people of the valley. Based on our promises, the people of the valley have been let down and destroyed by the National Energy Board report and the Berger report. Both of those reports were far from honest and far from objective.
This country has to get back to economics. We cannot afford to fiddle around any more with irrelevant issues, which is all we have done for ten years. This pipeline is a courtesy to a neighbour. Just as the Americans gave us the right to move Canadian oil from western Canada to the east through American territory, we should give them the same right. When we moved gas from western Canada, coming out of Manitoba, through the northern states and into Ontario, the Americans exacted conditions from us. In the Great Lakes application of 1966 they said we were spending all the money because it was our gas that was going through and that they wanted 50 per cent of the shares of the ownership, and they got it. We would not have got the pipeline otherwise. The U.S. government backs up American private companies. We accepted those conditions. If they want to move a pipeline through this country, we will help them in every way we can. We will do everything we can to facilitate it, even though it has been a farce to date.
I should like to refer to the advantage of it, which we do not understand, but the Americans, the Arabs and the Japenese do. When the Alberta Gas Trunk Pipeline Company was set up the provincial government moved and indicated that there would be five classes of shares, with so many shares going to the producing companies and so many shares going to the consuming companies, and that they would have votes. The government was to step in and buy two shares, and the public would be allowed the great majority of the shares if they lived in Alberta. Alberta people swarmed into the banks and the provincial treasury offices and bought many more shares than were available, and they had to be distributed pro rata. Today Alberta Gas Trunk is owned by the people of Alberta, but they do not have a vote in the company. The votes are left to the government.
During the past 20 years that company has operated without interference from the Alberta government. Relatively it is a very small company with a few hundred million dollars in assets, but it will now take over a $10 billion empire if this proposal for the Alcan route goes through. If they use the
August 5, 1977

same technique in controlling the massive investment which would go into this pipeline, $10 billion, you will find a little company like the Alberta Gas Company, a monopoly set up by the government of Alberta, with two shares owned by the government of Alberta, controlling this big entreprise to carry gas from American states to American states, and the people who are going to make the money will be those who hold the equity, because when you finance a pipeline it is traditional that you put so many shares out in equity, risk shares, and four or five or six times more in senior financing bonds. Suppose you have a conservative ratio of one to four. Those proportions are added together to make a rate base.
The total amount invested in equity and bonds is added together to give a rate base upon which the National Energy Board sets the rates of return. The Board usually sets a rate of return in the area of 9 per cent to 10 per cent. When they pay off the senior financing, the money paid to the pipeline company is the same as though the money had not been paid back as to bonds, and all the money ultimately goes to the shareholders. This is called a leverage situation. So if you have a one into four ratio, 20 per cent of the amount of participation at the beginning gets 100 per cent of the revenue. As a result, the value of the shares goes up five, six or seven times. This is the plum that every smart cookie in the whole world seeks. This is why the Americans asked for and got 80 per cent of the ownership of the TransCanada Pipeline when it started; this is why they asked for 50 per cent of the ownership of Great Lakes; this is why they asked 50 per cent of the ownership of West Coast Transmission in 1974.
When you know how many times you have been gored by men who understand the technique of oil pipeline financing you do not put yourself in a position to be gored again if you are smart. All the government has to do is think through the experience of West Coast in 1954 and of TransCanada Pipelines in 1956. Let members opposite read the debates which took place in this House in 1966 when the opposition persuaded the government to change its policy completely. If the government shows the strength to stand up, with all parties supporting it, and say they want equity to go to Canadians, they will get it. The Americans have no choice, because the only other option which faces them is to haul the gas down in pressurized ships specially constructed to carry liquid natural gas. This would add another chore to the work of the already hard-pressed American navy which cannot even keep peace in the Mediterranean. It would have to undertake the further task of seeking to protect a vital product going by sea. It is bad enough having to ask them to protect oil shipments.
Then, when the ships reach the west coast of the United States after all the expense of changing the natural into liquid form under great pressure, the cargo must be changed back to natural gas again to be sent to the people of Chicago through another pipeline costing $3 billion or $4 billion. Think of what the people of Chicago would have to pay for their own gas.
Northern Gas Pipeline
I go through the simple steps surrounding the financing of a pipeline to reinforce my plea to the House and to the government: please, don't let this chance slip by. Give Canadians an opportunity to get that first billion or billion and a half of equity. And when the project begins to pay off and the value of the shares goes up five or ten times we shall forgive the government for some of the mistakes it has made in the last 20 years. Think it through, let us not miss this opportunity. The Americans will have no argument to put up. They did it to us on the occasions I have mentioned.
I would ask for a lot more. I would say "You are going to need a paved highway to move all that stuff up along the Alcan route. We will build that highway and construct it to accommodate the big trucks needed to haul all that steel. But we want the Panhandle. That land was stolen from us in connivance with the British in 1906. We want it back."

don't get it back we want access to the sea. Lay down conditions. No Americans live in the Panhandle. It was put there specifically as a barrier, 25 miles east from tidewater, to keep us from the sea. And a great corner of North America is barred from the market because of that artificial, man-made barrier put up by the Americans and the British against Canada in 1906.
Oh yes, I would list a lot of conditions. We in the opposition have already listed seven or eight of them. But I have said enough to illustrate my point. Let us not be gored a fourth time in one generation. Three times is enough. Let us make some money out of the pipeline. That is what the Americans understand.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me say this: I have heard talk in this debate about a single agency to correlate all those 30 agencies which are involved in pipeline construction. I am not opposing that idea. It is a sensible one. But this operation amounts to an international treaty of an economic sort which will require a watchful eye on the part of the Canadian government and of all the Canadian interests involved for 30 years to come.
I believe it will be necessary to bring enabling legislation before the House to consider this whole project as being a 35 or 40-year deal, because if we leave it to the small holding companies, joined by ten or 15 operating companies, and give them monopolistic power to run this operation, in the absence of any control by the federal government we shall not be serving Canadian interests. Consider West Coast Transmission owned by the B.C. government, the Alberta Gas Company owned by the Alberta government, and the techniques of the operation of those two companies. If you put them in charge of this big pipeline it will be the same as putting a weasel in charge of a hen house.
Get the Canadian government into the picture. Make sure it has two or three directors on the board to see that Canadian interests are protected and that the operation is not run entirely by power hungry individuals who understand pipeline

financing. I am suggesting to the government that all is not lost. Let it get on the ball and act like Canadians for a change. Let Canadians have a chance to make a few dollars.
