speechtext:
The government has now consulted parliament. I believe we have taken our responsibility in doing so. Our responsibility now is to keep parliament informed, and eventually to let parliament decide whether it agrees with the form of that decision. That is the parliamentary process and the parliamentary system. I am sure the Leader of the Opposition would have been the first to criticize the government had the government House leader stood up yesterday and announced a decision.
One other speaker who I think should be singled out in the debate yesterday was the leader of the NDP (Mr. Broadbent). He adopted what can only be described as a ludicrous position for his party. It is the members of his party who had said that they wanted to have an input into the decision, that they wanted all members of parliament to have an input into the decision, or as many as could be heard, before the decision is taken. But what was the first thing he did? He placed an amendment before the House which in effect asks the House to take a decision before the House has even heard the views of members. Of course that is not the first time the NDP has adopted ludicrous positions.
My colleague, the government House leader, yesterday recited some of the events leading up to this debate. He spoke about the reports and the actions which gave existence to the reports: The Berger report, the NEB report, the Dean Lysyk report, the second Berger report, and the environmental assessment review process. He underlined as well the native interests and the concerns of the government with respect to those interests and the environmental interests with respect to a pipeline. He outlined the options for Canada and he also indicated rather strongly some of the complexities involved in reaching a decision of this magnitude.
I think it might be helpful to cast our minds back to the recent U.S. experience in Alaska. The U.S. has already experienced and faced up to environmental and native questions when it built the Alyeska line. Those complexities and difficulties with respect to the native claims and the environment were not insubstantial. There would be additional environmental problems for us if they were to decide to go for El Paso. Of course they would have to weigh the industrial benefits and the environmental costs which an El Paso route would involve against the lower prices and delivery to markets

August 5, 1977

of an overland Canadian route. This issue involves big money, big impact and big results, so it will not be settled overnight.
In concluding this debate I wish to place the spotlight for a moment on the question of energy supply and to summarize my impressions of the debate against the background of the major supply question for Canada.
The National Energy Board made reference to its 1975 report on natural gas supply requirements. It noted that some conditions have changed, basically as a result of the significantly higher prices which have brought supply and demand more in balance. Regrettably, the absence of assurances as to a secure supply-users will just not contract for gas without a five to ten years guarantee of supply-has resulted in an almost stagnant market for gas in Canada outside of Alberta in recent years. I call it regrettable because the prospects for oil production in Canada are much more serious. The alternatives are high cost tar sands and heavy oil production and imports.
I know a pipeline decision would clearly raise the question of how we provide that long term assurance of natural gas supplies which consumers and the distributing utilities need in order to plan for greater use of natural gas and less dependence on oil, particularly imported oil. It is thus not only a question of whether or not we need northern gas and, if so, when, but also whether or not we are going to indicate to natural gas users and potential users that there is a supply available not only in Alberta but also in the frontier. We need to be able to indicate to gas users that their investment is protected for its life, that they will not be cold if they decide to heat their homes and run their factories with natural gas.
We need to be able to indicate to potential gas users that the government's strategy is to use natural gas to the maximum extent wherever economical, and this requires the long term assurance of supply. Otherwise a major opportunity to replace foreign oil and to reduce our growing dependence on foreign oil will be severely threatened and forgone.
On the matter of the deliverability of gas, which in the final analysis is more important than a reserve estimate, I can say that analyses by my department and the National Energy Board on deliverability profiles show production from existing western Canada reserves peaking in 1981. When so-called trend gas is added, production will peak in 1983-84. After that time, amounts of trend gas deliverability cannot offset the decline in deliverability of the established reserves.
The Board has performed some very important sensitivity tests on its own projections of supply and demand. In one case when optimistic assumptions are used with respect to supply and a low growth rate for gas demand is assumed, an approximate balance between supply and demand, with no shortfalls, is obtained until the year 1990. I think it is important that we understand that. That is under one set of assumptions that the National Energy Board has used for this sensitivity analysis. I believe this points to the degree of uncertainty regarding the first year of shortfall, and, inasmuch as less than expected
Northern Gas Pipeline
supply trends and high demand growth could bring the supply-demand crossover point forward into the early 1980's, it does emphasize the importance of preparing for expected shortages well in advance rather than risking the country's energy supply on a fine calculation of a year or two of shortage. This is the fine tuning, in other words, into which some spokesmen have allowed themselves to be drawn. For this reason the board has emphasized the importance of frontier gas supply by the first half of the 1980's.
Finally, I would like to refer to some policy considerations relative to the supply and timing of Mackenzie Delta gas. In the report I released last year concerning our energy strategy for Canada emphasis was given to policies for self-reliance. Included in the policy elements are energy conservation and increased exploration and development. Those elements are directly related to curtailing demand growth and increasing energy supply to reduce the energy gap forecast for 1985. This remains our objective, and the opening up of new supply sources, whether in frontier areas or in the heavy oil areas of western Canada, is fundamental to the attainment of self-reliance.
The National Energy Board, after a very thorough and independent analysis, as I have said, has concluded that frontier gas supply before the mid-1980's is an essential element of the country's supply and demand equation. Here 1 must point out just one of perhaps several discrepancies in the positions taken by the Leader of the Opposition and his energy critic, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). On the one hand the Leader of the Opposition was saying "Damm the torpedoes, full speed ahead, we must have energy self-sufficiency by the year 1990". Bringing domestic demand, he said, into some kind of harmony by then was not only realizable but absolutely essential.
However, his energy critic, on the other hand, adopted a rather more relaxed attitude. He said that our need for frontier gas from the Delta or the Beaufort Sea will not come in the last half of the 1980's, or need not come. He said we should gamble. That was one of the words he used. He said we can get by without frontier gas until then. That was an incredibly rash statement, but any of us who have watched the hon. member for St. John's West in this House realize that was fully in character.

Nor am I suggesting that our energy conservation measures should be less stringent because we can achieve a supply and demand balance through new sources of supply. We must, in fact, increase our conservation efforts. The fact is that we are projecting an energy supply gap for 1985, even assuming frontier gas supplies and a considerable turnaround in the energy consumption habits of all Canadians. The alternative to greater self-reliance is an increasing dependence on imported oil. Forecasts of the world energy situation in the latter half of the next decade point to increasing competitive demand for decreasing supplies, and that can have only one result: escalating prices, very high prices or, at worst, a major security of supply problem.
While these supply conditions pertain to the mid-1980's and beyond, there is a tendency to forget about the long lead times involved in major resource development and transportation projects and to set aside the necessary decisions until it is too late to undertake a well planned program. This in turn often leads to crash programs which are costly and ineffective. The time for a decision on a northern pipeline is now. With a decision in principle preparations can be completed in a thorough manner and the facilities carefully constructed to open up new sources of energy supply for all Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had hoped to express my views in 20 minutes but understand I shall have available only two or three minutes. Therefore 1 have put aside my notes and will begin by commenting on the remarks of the minister. He commented on what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) said and also said, I think, that if we follow the counsel of the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) we shall face energy shortages in the years ahead. It is incredible that the minister who was in charge of energy affairs in this country when we were self-sufficient in energy, when reserves were growing, when our prospects for energy supplies were favourable, indeed excellent, should have brought this country to the position in which in the next five years it will be on its knees from the point of view of energy supplies. That is shameful.
Personally I believe the question of northern pipelines is greatly connected with the question of energy supplies in Canada. This point has been covered adequately; yet it is important to note that by 1980, in little more than two years, Canada will import some 390,000 barrels a day, according to figures the National Energy Board gave us, and by 1985, only about seven years away, Canada will depend on foreign sources for over half its oil. Given these projections and estimates as to where our future energy supplies will come from, we must look carefully at this country's pipelines.
The minister who is responsible for energy matters in Canada should reflect upon what others have said about energy to North America. Speaking on energy, the President
August 5, 1977

of the United States referred to it in April this year as the greatest challenge his country would face during our lifetime. He said the energy crisis has not yet overwhelmed us but it will if we do not act quickly. He said we must not be selfish or timid if we hope to have a decent world for our children and grandchildren. He concluded by saying we must simply balance our supply and demand for energy with our rapidly shrinking resources. By acting now we can control our future, instead of letting the future control us.
The minister referred again today to his strategies, his studies and to many reports. We have had, since the present minister and previous minister assumed the responsibility for their portfolios, nothing in the way of action. We have had all kinds of reports and heard a lot of talk. The minister speaks of the problems facing us but does nothing. Actually almost everything the government, including the minister, has done in the last few years with respect to energy has been negative, has in fact been a detriment to the acquisition of future supplies.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF PROPOSALS FOR NORTHERN GAS PIPELINE
speechtext: We have had government by regulation.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF PROPOSALS FOR NORTHERN GAS PIPELINE
speechtext:
An hon. member mentions rule by regulation. The government's actions in the area of energy are but another example of that rule. I do not think we have emphasized sufficiently in this debate the matter of Canada's security of future energy supplies. If we are to import about half our energy supplies, a substantial proportion will be shipped via the Indian Ocean and round South Africa. We shall be highly dependent on a number of foreign powers for our energy supplies. This, in addition to our economic difficulties, is a most serious problem to those of us who live in northern latitudes.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, it is very much in our interest to work together with the United States to make possible the construction of a northern pipeline. While we can be instrumental in making available to the United States sizable quantities of its own energy supplies, we can at the same time, probably by using the Dempster route, eventually bring into use our Mackenzie Delta and Beaufort Sea gas.
On reflecting on the events of the past months, after having visited recently the Mackenzie Delta, something I have done many times, I am impressed by a number of facts. For example, both natives and whites alike told me and my colleagues, when we visited the Delta, that Mr. Justice Berger's report does not properly represent the views of the northern people. The reason is, I think, that the views expressed to Mr. Justice Berger were largely those of a group of experts from Toronto, who arrived in the north on an aircraft ahead of Mr. Justice Berger and persuaded the natives as to what they should say. These same gentlemen probably wrote their reports right at the University of Toronto. We asked businessmen in the north why they did not put forward their views; or, why were we hearing from them views which had not been expressed to Mr. Justice Berger? The reason is this: the experts from Toronto were funded directly and indirectly by the government. They had funds which enabled them to sit at the hearings for days on end and to buy airline tickets which
Northern Gas Pipeline
are expensive items in northern communities. But the small businessmen, the young people who were enterprising and had staked their future in the north, had no chance to express their views, because they had neither the time nor the money to do it.
I can hardly fail to remind the House that Mr. Justice Berger himself at one time was an elected representative and formerly the leader of the New Democratic Party in British Columbia. As one northerner put it, asking Mr. Justice Berger to report on matters in the north is akin to appointing a cardinal to head a commission on abortion.
What are this country's energy reserves, and what are our potential sources of supply? We have a good deal of potential for supplies in Alberta. We have potential supplies off the east coast, but in deep water and probably cannot extract those supplies with presently known technology. I expect we shall need to learn new technologies. We have the Alberta oil sands and the heavy oils in Alberta. But the frontier area most likely to yield energy supplies immediately is the Mackenzie Delta.
We shall need all of this country's energy reserves. All will be required, each in their own time. The development of some can be hurried; the development of others cannot be. Huge sums of money will be required for exploration in our provinces and off the east coast. In view of the enormous costs of these developments, we shall need to time them carefully. Today we have known reserves in our western Arctic areas. The reports of the National Energy Board make clear that this area is the next and most important source which should be tapped for Canadian energy needs.
The projected production from the Mackenzie Delta would meet the growth in Canada's energy needs for less than two years. That should make it clear we shall need all our energy resources. We cannot stand aside at this time, awaiting the development of the oil sands, or the heavy oil reserves. We must make use of our present opportunity to bring on stream Mackenzie Delta gas.
It has been said in this debate that by agreeing to the pipeline we shall do the United States a favour. Before I deal with the point let me draw attention to the outstanding job done for many years by the Canadian Arctic gas group. This government told it to get to work and undertake studies in thousands of important areas. The group did its work well. It conducted undoubtedly one of the most thorough studies ever undertaken on northern ecological and transportation matters.
I ask again, who will be dealt a favour? I say that, yes, we can help the United States, and it is important for us to do so. But I also suggest this project is greatly to Canada's advantage. Today we desperately need the economic stimulus of this pipeline and its construction projects. This, of course, is largely due to the mess that our country is in as a result of the economic mismanagement of the government sitting opposite.
We cannot afford to build our own pipeline at the present time from our western Arctic reserves because they are not large enough. However, the Alaska-Yukon line which is pro-

Northern Gas Pipeline
posed by the Foothills group in Calgary to build their line within 480 miles of our reserves brings our reserves within reasonable distance of a major transportation artery. The energy supply of North America would be more secure and the strength of the economy of our largest trading partner would be increased.
Our supply of energy is important to us. Equally important to us is that the United States receives their supply of energy. Hon. members will recall how many Americans were out of jobs last winter and how seriously the slump in their economy affected Canada.
There is one other aspect. The pipeline group intends to employ thousands of people on the pipeline, something in the area of 5,000 or 6,000. This will be multiplied at least five times in other parts of Canada. That would be Hamilton, the maritimes, and as I told the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), they will probably eat a lot of fish in those pipeline camps.
I understand that another factor being considered is gas swaps. At the present time the important problem facing the United States is their short-term supply. The President of the United States has put into place a long term program but, as hon. members know, it takes a long lead time to bring these supplies on stream.
It is my understanding that affiliates of the Alaska-Yukon pipeline company are at the present time willing to deal with the United States on short-term supplies from western Canada. This is of considerable importance to the United States.
We have these additional supplies available. There appear to be various formulae to make possible their implementation. I urge the government to support these efforts and, wherever possible, to back those who are attempting to use these important levers to bring about acceptance by the United States of this particular route.
As I reflect on the figures of our own energy shortfalls in the eighties, I find them frightening. What is of even more concern is that the problem we have in energy is not truly an energy problem, but a political problem. It seems little short of incredible that Canada is programmed by this government in its studies to permit itself to lapse into heavy dependence on outside sources on the whims of foreign powers for its essential energy supply. It is all the more tragic when we realize that this potential energy is available in Canada through the various sources that we have.
There is the example of the northern regulations. This minister ought to be ashamed of himself. He has told this House and committee on more than two dozen occasions in the past six or eight months that these regulations would be available very soon. He said as recently as this past June that he would introduce them this session. We are well into the summer, and no regulations. This speaks very well for the concern the government has for the energy problem, and indeed the competence of the minister.
It is interesting that the government's program, the shortage and desperation in our actual supply situation, lead us very
much into the 1980's when we will be facing deficits which will not permit us to buy supplies. I wonder if the minister is aware of that.
Yesterday the Leader of the Opposition pointed out that studies by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and others clearly indicate that by the middle of the 1980's oil may very well not be available. This master plan, these studies, these words, all that we hear from this minister brings us to our maximum problem, our maximum shortages at the very time when world supplies will be phasing out and may very well be unavailable to us.
On the question of a northern pipeline, the government is obligated to come forward with some answers. It has had this problem for many years. The opportunity to build an oil line through Canada came at the time that Alaska oil was to be brought from Alaska. The government failed to react. It said no. It had an opportunity at that time to take steps to make possible the energy corridors, but it failed miserably. It is continuing to do so.
